title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
1 · What you hear → · Glossary
A piano note has a pitch you could hum; a drum’s thud has none. Both are a stretched, struck piece of material. This series explains the difference with one piece of mathematics, the spectrum of an operator, and it is organised around four questions:

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The posts

What you hear answers questions 1 and 2, with sounds and no differential equations. A clear pitch means the partials sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, so the sound nearly repeats at that rate; a piano’s partials very nearly do this and a drum’s don’t.
Where the equations come from answers question 3. For small motions, Newton’s law on a small piece, together with a law of the material, gives u_{tt} = -Au, with an operator A for each object: spring, beads, string, air column, bar, stiff string, drumhead, and a coil with a capacitor.
When an equation has a spectrum answers question 4, the mathematical answer. The solutions of U' = BU are exactly the combinations of modes when B has a basis of eigenvectors; for a stable, frictionless object of finite size this always holds (once any rigid drift is split off), and the post shows where it fails.
Instruments, case by case puts the answers to work on one instrument per page, starting from an orchestra: violin, clarinet, kalimba, harmonica, piano, bass drum and kettledrum.

Two further posts take up questions the answers raise: Can you hear the shape of a drum? and Did instruments shape our scales?. A Piano is a playable upright with all 88 keys and its three pedals. Technical words link to the glossary.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The series in one paragraph
A vibrating object of finite size whose motion is linear and unchanging in time moves, left to itself, as a sum of modes, apart from the special cases post 3 lists: shapes that each oscillate at their own frequency f_k and fade with their own time \tau_k. The body, the air and the room pass that motion on to a listener in a way that is also linear and unchanging in time: this keeps every f_k and \tau_k, changes the amounts, and adds the filter’s own ringing (the body’s resonances, the room’s reverberation). So the instrument’s part of the sound is 
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\, e^{-t/\tau_k} \cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k).
 The equation of motion (the operator, together with friction and radiation) fixes the f_k and \tau_k; the playing, the radiation and where you listen fix the a_k. The four aspects are heard from these lists, through the ear’s own weighting: pitch mainly from where the f_k sit; loudness from the sizes, weighted by frequency; timbre from all three lists, especially early on, plus noise that is not a mode; duration from the fading and from when the player stops or damps the note. Bowed and blown instruments are different: their motion is a single repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples; the resonator’s modes shape which partials are strong, and the player sets loudness and duration.
The series derives the f_k; the \tau_k are mostly measured, and it says so where it uses them.
Here p(t) is the air pressure at the listener; a_k is how strongly the k-th partial sounds, \varphi_k where in its cycle it starts, and e^{-t/\tau_k} says that it shrinks by a factor of e \approx 2.7 every \tau_k seconds.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
Operator families and instrument classes
The Hornbostel–Sachs classification, the scheme most used by those who study instruments, sorts them into five classes by what makes the sound. This series groups them by operator family: instruments whose operators agree up to constants and how they are held, so that one calculation covers them all.

Hornbostel–Sachs class, instrument, operator family, and the posts that derive the operator (2) and hear the instrument (4).

DetailsThe decimal codes, and when electrophones were added

The numbers are the scheme’s decimal codes, read from the left. Among the chordophones (3), 321.322 are necked box lutes, such as the violin (bowed, 321.322-71) and the guitar; 322 are harps; 314.122 are board zithers with a resonator box, where the piano sits, as 314.122-4-8, sounded by hammers from a keyboard. Among the aerophones (4), 421.121.12 are open side-blown flutes with fingerholes; 422.211.2 are clarinets with a cylindrical bore and fingerholes; 412.132 are sets of free reeds, inside the interruptive free aerophones (412), where “the air-stream is interrupted periodically”. Among the idiophones (1), 122.1 are plucked idiophones in the form of a comb, with laced-on lamellae (thin tongues), and 111.222 are sets of struck percussion plaques. Among the membranophones (2), 211.11 are single kettle drums and 211.212.1 single cylindrical drums with two heads. Number 531.1 places the theremin in 53, Sachs’s group of radioelectric instruments, those that make their sound with electrically driven oscillators.
Hornbostel and Sachs published the scheme in 1914 with four classes; electrophones came later. Francis Galpin gave them a class of their own in his own scheme (1937), and Sachs added them to Hornbostel–Sachs as a fifth class, with the groups 51 to 53, in The History of Musical Instruments (1940). Anthony Baines and Klaus Wachsmann’s English translation (1961) keeps the four classes of 1914 (Lee 2020).





DetailsWhat varies inside one operator family

Inside one operator family the rule stays and the rest varies:

Strings and air columns, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2. What moves, the string’s height or the air’s pressure; the constants that set the lowest frequency, such as length, tension and mass per length; the ends, which are part of the operator: tied, open at both ends (flute) or closed at one (clarinet, pan pipes); and the playing: plucked (guitar, harp), bowed (violin) or blown.
Bending bars, \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4. Steel tine, brass reed or metal bar; the ends, one clamped or both free, which change the frequency ratios; and the playing: plucked, struck or blown, which decides whether you hear the bar’s own overtones or the whole-number multiples of a steady airflow.
Stiff strings, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4. The stiffness, whose effect is largest at the two ends of a piano’s keyboard (the piano page).
Membranes, -c^2\Delta. Tension and size, and what surrounds the head, which matters for timpani.
A single number, such as k/m for a mass on a spring or 1/LC for a coil and a capacitor. Nothing varies but the number.






DetailsWhere the classes and the mathematics part ways

Hornbostel–Sachs asks what makes the sound; the operator asks what oscillates and by what rule. Mostly the answers line up. Where they part, the difference is instructive.

The piano is a chordophone, a board zither whose strings are struck by hammers, but its operator adds the bar’s fourth derivative to the string’s, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4: its steel wire is stiff enough to bend like a bar (the piano page).
The harmonica is an aerophone, classed by its interrupted airstream, though its reed is a clamped bar like the kalimba’s tine. That agrees with the harmonica page: the steady sound has only whole-number multiples of the puff rate, set by the chopped airflow, and the reed’s own off-line overtones are absent from it.
The glockenspiel and the kalimba are idiophones in different groups, struck and plucked, and in one operator family. They share the rule \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, but their ends differ, both free for the glockenspiel bar and one clamped for the tine, so their operators differ, and so do their frequency ratios, 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 against 1 : 6.27 : 17.55.
A violin string and a flute’s air column are in different classes, yet their operators agree up to constants, so they are in one operator family: both are -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 with the value held at zero at both ends, the string’s height at its tied ends and the air’s extra pressure at the flute’s open ends (post 2).
An electric guitar is a chordophone with a pickup: its strings make the sound, and the electronics only pick it up and amplify it.
A theremin is an electrophone: its oscillators are coil-and-capacitor circuits, whose operator is the single number 1/LC; post 2 derives it and explains how the player’s hand sets the pitch.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
Did instrument makers know?
Mostly not. The mathematics in this series explained instruments after they were built: makers found what works by trying and listening, and the theory came later, often much later. Bell founders tuned each bell’s partials by ear and lathe for the Zutphen carillon of 1644; experimenters found the laws of strings (Mersenne, 1636) and the still points of a vibrating string (Noble and Pigot, 1670s; Sauveur, 1701). The wave equation (d’Alembert, 1747), modes and their superposition (Daniel Bernoulli, Euler, Fourier) and the spectral theory behind this series (Sturm and Liouville, Rayleigh, Hilbert, Weyl) followed. Designing an instrument by computing its spectrum before it is made is recent: computed marimba bar profiles appear around 1990, and a bell with a major third was designed by finite-element computation in the 1980s.



DetailsThe longer story, with sources

Instruments came first. How Antonio Stradivari made his violins is not documented, so saying that he worked by trial and ear is an inference. Bells show trial and ear at work more plainly. The blind Utrecht carillonneur Jacob van Eyck picked out the separate partials of a bell by whistling at them, and held that a bell must be tuned after casting by changing its shape. In 1644 the city of Zutphen ordered a carillon from the founders Pieter and François Hemony, with van Eyck as its adviser. The brothers cast the bells slightly too thick, turned each on a lathe and shaved metal from the inside until its five principal partials were in tune. The Zutphen carillon is counted as the first tuned carillon.
Laws from experiment. The Pythagorean tradition tied consonant intervals to simple ratios of string lengths: half the length sounds an octave higher. In the late 1580s Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo’s father, hung weights on strings and found that tension works differently: an octave needs four times the weight and a fifth 9 : 4, so the frequency goes with the square root of the tension. Marin Mersenne’s Harmonie universelle (1636) stated the laws of a string together: its frequency is inversely proportional to its length, proportional to the square root of its tension and inversely proportional to the square root of its mass per length, as in f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu} on post 2. In Oxford in the mid-1670s William Noble and Thomas Pigot found that a string can vibrate in parts with still points between them: small pieces of paper hung on the string stayed at rest at some points and trembled at others. John Wallis reported the discovery in the Philosophical Transactions in 1677. In 1701 Joseph Sauveur explained such motions to the Paris Academy: a string can vibrate at higher frequencies, which he called harmonics, separated by still points, which he called nodes. Both words are still in use.
The mathematics, after the fact. Brook Taylor (1713) worked out from mechanics the shape and the period of a string’s simplest vibration. Jean le Rond d’Alembert (1747) wrote down the wave equation and solved it as two waves running in opposite directions. Daniel Bernoulli (1753) stated that the general motion of a vibrating system is a superposition of its modes; Euler, d’Alembert and Lagrange did not accept that sums of sines could match an arbitrary starting shape. Leonhard Euler worked out the vibrations of a drumhead (published 1766), and the functions now named after Bessel appear there for every whole-number order; the simplest, J_0, had already turned up in Daniel Bernoulli’s hanging chain in the 1730s. Ernst Chladni (1787) made the nodal lines of vibrating plates visible with sand. Joseph Fourier, in a memoir of 1807 and a book of 1822, argued that any function can be written as a sum of sines and cosines, and used such sums to solve the equation of heat flow. Charles Sturm and Joseph Liouville (1836–37) developed expansions of this kind for a whole class of second-order equations, the eigenvalue problems now named after them. Karl Weierstrass (1858) corrected a conclusion of Lagrange, repeated by Laplace and others: they had held that two equal frequencies would make a small oscillation grow with time, and Weierstrass showed that for small oscillations about a stable rest they do not. Lord Rayleigh’s The Theory of Sound (1877) gathered the subject into one treatise. David Hilbert’s work on integral equations in the 1900s introduced the name spectral theory, and Hermann Weyl (1911) proved that the frequencies of a drum determine its area (Can you hear the shape of a drum?).
Computed design is recent. A marimba bar is thinned by an arch cut under its middle. The arch lowers the lowest frequency more than the overtones, and so moves the first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, the uniform bar of Did instruments shape our scales?, up to a whole-number multiple, usually 4. Makers such as J. C. Deagan’s company in Chicago, building marimbas from the early 1900s, and later Clair Omar Musser’s, tuned each bar by grinding the arch and checking the result, by ear and with pitch-measuring devices as they appeared, such as Deagan’s own “Deagan-o-meter” (1915) and the strobe tuner (1936). The shape of the arch was found by trial. Bar profiles computed in advance, before any wood or metal is cut, appear in the acoustics literature around 1990 (Orduña-Bustamante, 1991). Bells followed the same path. A traditional tuned bell has a minor third among its main partials. In the 1980s engineers at the Eindhoven University of Technology designed a bell with a major third instead, by finite-element computation and structural optimization, and the Eijsbouts bell foundry cast it.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 4 · Instruments, case by case · Beyond · Did instruments shape our scales? → · Glossary
Listen first: play each drum with every mode equally loud. Then click a drum to strike it at a point, and compare.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: the Laplacian (post 2), and counting.
This page asks what the spectrum says about the drum. First, the equation, which post 2 derived step by step.
Let the drumhead be a region \Omega of the plane, in one piece, and let u(x, y, t) be the height of the head above the point (x, y) at time t. In post 2, Newton’s law for one small patch of the head, pulled by the tension in its edges, gave the drum’s equation 
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \ \text{ on the rim},
 where \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} is the Laplacian, and c^2 is the tension divided by the mass per unit area. The Laplacian is positive where u at a point sits below the average of u around it, and negative where it sits above; the bigger the gap, the bigger the Laplacian. So the equation says: each point of the head accelerates toward the average height around it.
What we assumed, as for the drumhead in post 2: small slopes, a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, no air, and no damping.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
2 · The operator
In the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u, the operator is A = -c^2\Delta, acting on shapes that are zero on the rim. The rim condition is part of the operator: the same rule on a different shape is a different operator.

The drum’s operator: A = -c^2\Delta on the drumhead \Omega, acting on shapes with u = 0 on the rim.
In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point of the head back toward rest is c^2 times how far that point sits from the average around it.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
When is there a mode? A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X, with \lambda the eigenvalue. Write \lambda = c^2 k^2, so that the shape must satisfy 
-\Delta X = k^2 X \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad X = 0 \ \text{ on the rim}.
 The numbers k^2 for which this has a solution other than X = 0 are the eigenvalues of -\Delta on \Omega, and the solutions X are its eigenfunctions, the mode shapes. They depend only on the shape \Omega; the factor c^2 only scales them.
List them. Put the eigenvalues in order, k_1^2 \le k_2^2 \le k_3^2 \le \cdots, each repeated as many times as it occurs (its multiplicity). The mode with k_n^2 has the operator’s eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 and swings at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{c\,k_n}{2\pi}.


The drum’s spectrum: the eigenvalues \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 of A, where -\Delta X_n = k_n^2 X_n inside \Omega and X_n = 0 on the rim, listed \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots with repeats. The frequencies are f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = c\,k_n/2\pi.
In words: apart from the one overall factor c, the frequencies are decided by the shape of \Omega alone.

Kac’s question, precisely. Suppose we know c, so that hearing every frequency means knowing every k_n^2. Does the list k_1^2, k_2^2, k_3^2, \dots determine \Omega? It can only do so up to sliding, turning or flipping the drum, which changes no frequency. (Kac wrote that he had first heard the question posed this way about ten years earlier, from Salomon Bochner.)

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Here are both drums’ first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, \sqrt{\lambda_n/\lambda_1} = k_n/k_1: 1×, 1.20×, 1.43×, 1.60×, 1.69×, 1.90×, 2.04×, …. Like the drum on the drum page, they sit off the gray whole-number lines, so neither drum has a clear pitch. And the two lists are the same to every digit computed: the stems under drum A and drum B stand in the same places. In the demo, each stem’s height is how strongly a strike at the clicked point starts that mode (below, every mode is drawn equally tall): all equal until you click, then different on the two drums, because it depends on the mode’s shape at the struck point.


  
  Both drums' first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, every mode drawn equally tall: drum A and drum B have exactly these stems (Driscoll's values).

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
5 · What we hear
Same frequencies, not the same sound. A struck drum moves as a sum of its modes, 
u = \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n),
 so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n, each fading at its own rate, with a strength a_n that depends on where it is struck; what you hear also depends on where you listen. The demo’s sound is made exactly this way, from the frequencies in stage 3. The two drums share the frequencies f_n. The mode shapes X_n differ, so the strengths from a strike at a given point differ, and so does the timbre, the color of the sound. Played with every mode equally loud, every a_n = 1, the two drums sound identical. What the drums share is the answer to “which frequencies can this drum make”, which is exactly what the spectrum records.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What the spectrum knows
Counting the frequencies: area and rim. Count the eigenvalues of -\Delta up to a limit \Lambda: 
N(\Lambda) = \#\{n : k_n^2 \le \Lambda\},
 where \# means “the number of”. (A frequency limit f corresponds to \Lambda = (2\pi f/c)^2, since f_n = c\,k_n/2\pi.) For a high limit, 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\,\Lambda \;-\; \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt{\Lambda},
 where |\Omega| is the drum’s area and P the length of its rim. In words: the number of modes below a high limit grows in proportion to the area, so twice the area gives about twice as many modes; and it falls short of the area’s share by an amount in proportion to the rim’s length, because holding the rim still costs the drum some modes.
The first term is Weyl’s law. Hermann Weyl proved it in 1911, and later work extended it to every drum. So the area can be heard: it is 4\pi times the rate at which N(\Lambda) grows. The second term is subtler. For the count itself it is proved only for some drums: Victor Ivrii proved it in 1980 for smooth rims on which closed billiard paths are rare (fold below). For a slightly smoothed version of the count it is proved for every drum whose rim is smooth or made of straight pieces, and that is enough to hear the rim’s length. Where the second term holds, “\approx” means that the error, divided by \sqrt\Lambda, shrinks to zero as \Lambda grows.
The demo counts the modes of three drums with the same area. Once the area’s share, the same for all three, is taken away, the drum with the longest rim sits lowest.


  
  
    Modes below the limit
    Minus the area's share
  
  Frequency limit
  
  Three drums of equal area: a disk, a square, a long rectangle. Steps: the true counts. Dashed: Weyl's formula, area and rim together. Gray: the area's share alone, the same for all three.





PreciselyWhat the demo plots, and Ivrii’s condition on billiard paths uses limits

In the demo all three drums have area |\Omega| = \pi (a disk of radius 1, a square, and a rectangle 4 times as long as it is wide), so the area’s share is \Lambda/4, and “minus the area’s share” plots N(\Lambda) - \Lambda/4, roughly -P\sqrt\Lambda/4\pi: the longer the rim, the lower the curve. The demo’s frequency limit is shown as a multiple of the disk’s lowest frequency, \sqrt{\Lambda}/k_1.
Ivrii’s condition: a billiard path is the path of a ball rolling inside the drum and bouncing off the rim, angle in equal to angle out; it is closed if it comes back to where it started, heading the same way. “Rare” means that if you pick a starting point and a direction at random, the chance of landing on a closed path is zero. Ivrii conjectured that this always holds; it has not been proved. The square and the rectangle in the demo have corners, which his theorem does not cover, but for them the formula can be checked by counting, as in the next fold. The perimeter can be heard in any case, for every drum whose rim is smooth or a polygon, by a smoother way of counting; that is the fold after it.





Proof sketchWeyl’s law for a square, by counting dots uses partial derivatives

Take the square of side s. Its eigenfunctions of -\Delta are \sin(m\pi x/s)\sin(n\pi y/s) for whole numbers m, n \ge 1, with eigenvalues k^2 = (\pi/s)^2(m^2 + n^2); substituting them into the equation checks this, as for the loop of string in post 3. So N(\Lambda) is the number of dots (m, n), with m, n \ge 1, inside the quarter circle of radius R = s\sqrt\Lambda/\pi.















RR

Give each dot the unit square centered on it. These squares nearly fill the quarter disk, which has area \pi R^2/4. What they miss is a strip of width \tfrac12 along each axis, of area about R/2 each, shaded in the figure; the squares sticking out past the arc and the gaps inside it roughly cancel. So 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{\pi R^2}{4} - R = \frac{s^2}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{4s}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda .
 In the figure, R = 5.3: there are 17 dots, and the formula gives 16.8. The strips are missing because m = 0 and n = 0 give the zero function, not an eigenfunction: the rim’s condition u = 0 is what costs the perimeter term. Making “roughly cancel” precise is a classical problem about counting lattice points in a circle.





Proof sketchHearing the perimeter of a drum with a smooth or straight-sided rim: a smoother count uses the heat equation and a mirror-image trick

N(\Lambda) jumps by one at every eigenvalue, and those jumps can bunch up, which is what Ivrii’s condition controls. A smoother count avoids them. For t > 0 let 
Z(t) = \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.
 Each eigenvalue adds nearly 1 if k_n^2 is much less than 1/t and nearly 0 if it is much more, so Z(t) is roughly N(1/t), with the jumps smoothed out. Like N, Z is determined by the list of eigenvalues.
Z has a physical meaning. Heat spreading on the drumhead, with the rim held at temperature 0, obeys v_t = \Delta v, the drum’s equation with one time derivative instead of two, so each mode now decays like e^{-k_n^2 t} instead of oscillating. Start a unit burst of heat at a point x and let it spread for time t. The temperature it leaves at x itself, added up over all points x of the drum, is Z(t). (Write the burst as a sum of modes, each scaled so that \iint X_n^2\,dA = 1. A burst at x contains mode n in proportion to X_n(x), the same rule as a strike on the drum page; after time t that part has shrunk by e^{-k_n^2 t}, and its temperature at x is again proportional to X_n(x). So the temperature left at x is \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}X_n(x)^2, and adding it up over the drum gives \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.) In a short time t heat travels a distance of about \sqrt t, so a burst only feels the rim if it starts within about that distance of it. Kac called this “not feeling the boundary”. Then:

Away from the rim, the burst spreads as on an endless plane, and the temperature it leaves at its starting point is 1/(4\pi t). Adding this up over the drum gives |\Omega|/(4\pi t).
Near a straight piece of rim, at distance r from it, the rim’s condition v = 0 is met by adding a mirror-image burst of opposite sign on the far side of the rim; a wave on a string meets a tied end the same way, as if an upside-down mirror image arrived from beyond it. The image is a distance 2r away, and lowers the temperature at x by e^{-r^2/t}/(4\pi t). Adding this up over a strip along the rim, using \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/t}\,dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi t} for each unit of rim length, gives -P/(8\sqrt{\pi t}).

So, as t \to 0, 
Z(t) = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi t} - \frac{P}{8\sqrt{\pi t}} + (\text{terms that stay bounded}).
 Knowing Z, one reads off |\Omega| from the first term and then P from the second. Kac gave this argument in his 1966 paper. Åke Pleijel had already proved the formula for smooth rims in 1954, by another method; Henry McKean and Isadore Singer proved in 1967 the next, constant term, which Kac had conjectured, from an argument that was not a full proof: (1 - h)/6 for a drum with h holes and a smooth rim; and Michiel van den Berg and Sivakolundu Srisatkunarajah proved the formula for polygons in 1988. Unlike N, Z needs no condition on billiard paths, because averaging over a range of eigenvalues smooths out the bunching.


So a round drum can be heard. Of all shapes with the same area, the disk has the shortest rim. This is the isoperimetric inequality: every drum satisfies 
P^2 \ge 4\pi\,|\Omega|,
 with equality only for the disk. Both sides can be heard, for a rim that is smooth or made of straight pieces. So a drum with such a rim that has exactly a disk’s frequencies has the disk’s area and rim length, so P^2 = 4\pi|\Omega|, so it is a disk. Kac pointed this out in section 10 of his 1966 paper: “By pitch alone one can thus determine whether a drum is circular or not!”
But in general, no. Two years before Kac’s paper, John Milnor had found two different shapes with the same frequencies, and Kac said so; but they were 16-dimensional and had no rim. (They are flat tori: 16-dimensional versions of a video-game screen whose edges wrap around, so that leaving on the right brings you back on the left.) For drums in the plane the question stayed open for 26 years. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert answered it: no. They found two different polygons with exactly the same frequencies, repeats included: the two drums at the top of this page. Such drums are called isospectral. Since area and rim length can be heard, they must share them, and they do: each is made of seven copies of the same right triangle, with two short sides of length 1, so each has area 3.5 and rim length 6 + 3\sqrt2.
Why do they share every frequency? Cut each drum into its seven triangles. Any mode of drum A can be rebuilt on drum B: fill each of B’s triangles with three triangle-shaped pieces of the mode, taken from A’s triangles, turned or flipped to fit, some with their signs reversed. With the right choice of pieces and signs, they join smoothly across every seam and stay still on B’s rim, so the result is a mode of B, at the same frequency. The construction runs backwards too, so the two drums have exactly the same frequencies, with the same number of modes at each.



DetailsTransplantation: carrying a mode from one drum to the other uses the Laplacian (post 2)

Cut each drum along its seams into its seven triangles. Take any eigenfunction X of drum A, with -\Delta X = k^2 X. On each triangle of drum B, place a sum of three pieces of X, each taken from one of A’s triangles, turned or reflected to fit, and some with a minus sign. Each piece satisfies -\Delta X = k^2 X, so the sum does too, inside each triangle. With the right choice of pieces and signs, the result is zero on B’s rim, and across every seam of B both its values and its slopes match. A function that satisfies the equation on both sides of a line, with values and slopes matching on the line, satisfies it across the line too, a standard fact about this equation. At the points where several seams meet, one more standard fact closes the gap: a solution that stays bounded around a single point, and satisfies the equation everywhere near it except possibly at the point itself, satisfies it there too. So the result is an eigenfunction of B with the same k^2, and so the same frequency. The construction can be reversed, so each eigenvalue has the same multiplicity on both drums.
This argument is called transplantation. It grew out of work of Peter Buser on surfaces in the 1980s and of Pierre Bérard around 1992; the version for drums like these is in a 1994 paper of Buser, John Conway, Peter Doyle and Klaus-Dieter Semmler. The seven formulas, with pictures, are in Cleve Moler’s blog post on transplantation, and in S. J. Chapman’s article, which does the same by folding paper. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s own proof used a method of Toshikazu Sunada from 1985 for building isospectral spaces from group theory; Wikipedia has an overview.





DetailsHow the numbers on this page were computed uses matrices, as for the beads in post 2

Each drum is covered by a square grid of spacing h, and the Laplacian is replaced by its five-point version: at each grid point, the sum of the four neighbors minus four times the point, divided by h^2. This is the bead model of post 2 in two dimensions. Grid points on the rim are held at zero. The drums’ corners sit on grid points, so whether each point is inside, on the rim, or outside is decided with exact whole-number arithmetic.
At h = 1/40 and h = 1/80 the two drums give the same first twelve eigenvalues k_n^2 of -\Delta to a relative difference of 3\times10^{-14}, which is rounding error. This is expected, as far as I can tell, because the grid lines up with every triangle’s edges, so transplantation works for the grid model too; Moler’s post transplants grid eigenvectors in the same way. Combining the two grids (Richardson extrapolation) gives values within 0.03% of the high-accuracy values in Table 3.1 of Driscoll’s paper, after multiplying his by 4: his drums are twice the size of these. That is a check, not a precise computation: Richardson’s trick assumes the grid error shrinks like h^2, and the drums’ inward-pointing corners slow that down. The page uses Driscoll’s values.
One eigenvalue is known exactly, the ninth, k_9^2. Its mode is, on each triangle, that triangle’s own lowest mode, \sin\pi x\,\sin 2\pi y - \sin 2\pi x\,\sin\pi y in coordinates where the triangle has corners (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1), with its sign flipping across each seam. Substituting gives k_9^2 = \pi^2(1 + 4) = 5\pi^2 = 49.348\ldots, and Driscoll’s value agrees to every digit he gives. On the grid, the ninth eigenvalue equals the grid version of this mode’s eigenvalue to rounding error, a second check.
The scripts are gww.py for the eigenvalues and gww_modes.py for the mode pictures. The corner coordinates are those in Moler’s first post. The mode pictures use the coarser grid h = 1/40, sampled every 0.1.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What we found
A drum’s spectrum, the eigenvalues of A = -c^2\Delta with the rim held still, tells you its area through Weyl’s law and, for a smooth or straight-sided rim, the length of its rim, which is enough to recognize a round drum. It does not always tell you the shape: Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s two drums share every frequency, though struck at a point they sound different. The study of what a spectrum says about the shape behind it is called spectral geometry; the last page asks what a spectrum says about music.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 2 · Where the equations come from · 4 · Instruments, case by case → · Glossary
The question. When is the motion a differential equation describes a sum of modes, with frequencies read off the spectrum of an operator; what theory lies behind that; and how does it connect back to what we hear?
The series in one paragraph

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
0 · Recap: the equation of motion
Post 2 derives the equations of motion; this post needs their form and a few cases.
The operator. For an object held in a given way, the operator A is the linear map, defined on the shapes that the holding allows, that sends a shape to minus the acceleration that shape causes. It does not depend on time. Linear means A(au + bv) = a\,Au + b\,Av for shapes u, v and numbers a, b. Newton’s law for small motions reads 
u'' = -A\,u ,
 with u(t) the shape at time t and primes time derivatives. Convention: A includes its constants, \lambda is an eigenvalue of A, f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi.
One mass on a spring (post 2). Hooke’s law gives m\,x'' = -k\,x, so A is the number k/m.
Two beads on a string (post 2). Two beads of mass m sit on a string of tension T, spaced h apart and h from the tied ends, at heights x_1 and x_2.

  
  
  
  
  x₁x₂ends tied
  
  
  12closed into a ring

For small slopes, each stretch of string pulls the two beads at its ends toward each other with vertical force T/h times their difference in height, a tied end counting as a bead at height 0. Newton’s law for each bead, with the heights in one column x = (x_1, x_2), becomes 
\begin{gathered}
m\,x_1'' = \frac{T}{h}\,(-2x_1 + x_2), \qquad m\,x_2'' = \frac{T}{h}\,(x_1 - 2x_2), \\
\text{that is}\qquad x'' = -A\,x, \qquad A = \frac{T}{mh}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} .
\end{gathered}

Continuous objects (post 2’s table), used in section 5:

The operators of post 2. Primes here are derivatives in position; \Delta = \partial_x^2 + \partial_y^2 is the Laplacian.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
1 · The smallest examples
The spring: one mode. In x'' = -\lambda x with \lambda = k/m, try x = a\cos(\omega t + \varphi). Two derivatives give -\omega^2x, which matches when \omega^2 = \lambda: the mass swings at f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi, whatever the amplitude a and phase \varphi, which the start fixes. One eigenvalue, one mode, one frequency.
Two beads: two modes. Add and subtract the bead equations. The sum S = x_1 + x_2 and the difference D = x_1 - x_2 obey 
S'' = -\frac{T}{mh}\,S, \qquad D'' = -\frac{3T}{mh}\,D :
 two independent springs, the second three times as stiff because in D the tilted middle stretch pulls too. In matrix language, (1, 1) and (1, -1) are eigenvectors of A, columns that A only rescales, with eigenvalues T/mh and 3T/mh: in the ratio 1 : 3, so the frequencies are in the ratio 1 : \sqrt 3 \approx 1 : 1.73. Since x_1 = (S + D)/2 and x_2 = (S - D)/2, every motion is an S-swing plus a D-swing.


  
    
    
  
  
    Together, S
    Opposite, D
    A mix
     close into a ring
    Hear this motion
  
  Slowed down. Tied ends: S swings at 1×, D at 1.73× (√3). Closed into a ring: nothing pulls S back; started at rest, it just stays shifted (a constant displacement), and D swings at 2×. On the right, the plane of the two heights (x₁ across, x₂ up): the path of a mix is a tangle, while S and D each run straight along their own tilted line. The model has no friction; the sound, with S at 196 Hz, fades only so that it stops.


The two-bead ring: a drift. Join the string’s ends to each other and each bead has the other as its neighbor on both sides: A_{\text{ring}} = \frac{T}{mh}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right), a different operator for the same beads. Now A_{\text{ring}}(1, 1) = 0: both beads move up together and nothing pulls back. Started moving, it drifts away silently, x = (1, 1)(a + bt). The other eigenvalue is 4T/mh.
The loop of string: exactly on the whole numbers. Join a continuous string into a loop, and measure position by the angle \theta, in units where the circumference is 2\pi. Post 2’s string equation becomes 
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu},
 on shapes that close up after one turn, X(\theta + 2\pi) = X(\theta); subscripts are partial derivatives. A mode’s shape satisfies AX = \lambda X, that is, X'' = -(\lambda/c^2)\,X (primes in \theta). For \lambda = c^2k^2 > 0 (here k is a wavenumber, not the spring’s stiffness), X = a\cos k\theta + b\sin k\theta, which closes up exactly when k is a whole number n. For \lambda = 0, X = a + b\theta closes up only if b = 0: the whole loop lifted, no sound. No \lambda is negative (fold). So mode n, with eigenfunctions \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta, sounds at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{nc}{2\pi} = n\,f_1 ,
 exactly a whole-number multiple of the lowest, for two reasons. Each wave has a whole number of crests, because it must close up. And every wave travels at the same speed: u = g(\theta - ct) solves the equation for every shape g, since u_{tt} and c^2u_{\theta\theta} both equal c^2g''. Mode n is two such waves running in opposite directions, \cos n\theta\cos nct = \tfrac12\cos n(\theta - ct) + \tfrac12\cos n(\theta + ct), whose n crests pass a fixed point n times while one crest goes around. On beads short waves are slower, on a stiff piano wire faster; both leave the whole numbers.


  
  Beads
  
  
  Hear the first modes together
  A ring of beads with the loop's size, tension and total mass, the mass shared among more and more beads. Stems: the first ten frequencies, as multiples of the lowest; the slider's last position is the continuous loop, where every stem sits on its line. Higher modes are drawn and played quieter, so they are not shrill; the lowest plays at 196 Hz.


Every shape is a sum of these waves, its Fourier series f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n\ge1}(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta) (the amounts, and in what sense, in the fold). Released from rest, each wave swings at its own frequency, u(\theta, t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_n (a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta)\cos(nct), so the motion repeats every 2\pi/c, and so does its sound (post 1).



PreciselyNo negative eigenvalues, and in what sense every shape is a sum of waves uses complex numbers and analysis

No negative eigenvalue. If X'' = qX with q > 0 on the loop, multiply by X and integrate over one turn. Integration by parts, with no boundary terms on a closed loop, gives \int X''X\,d\theta = -\int (X')^2\,d\theta \le 0, while q\int X^2\,d\theta \ge 0. Both are then zero, so X = 0.
The amounts. For a shape f of the loop, 
\begin{gathered}
f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta\big), \\
a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f\cos n\theta\,d\theta, \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f\sin n\theta\,d\theta .
\end{gathered}
 The amounts come from perpendicularity: \int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for n \ne m, likewise for sines and for a sine against a cosine, so multiplying by \cos m\theta and integrating leaves \pi a_m. Whether every shape, a plucked corner included, is such a sum was argued over from the 1740s by d’Alembert, Euler and Daniel Bernoulli and settled much later.
The series. With Euler’s formula e^{in\theta} = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta, the series reads f = \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} c_n e^{in\theta} with c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta, so c_{\pm n} = (a_n \mp i b_n)/2 for n \ge 1 and c_0 = a_0/2. The functions e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi} form an orthonormal basis of L^2(S^1), the functions on the circle with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite, for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\bar g\,d\theta: for every f in L^2(S^1), 
\Big\| f - \sum_{|n|\le M} c_n e^{in\theta}\Big\| \to 0 \quad (M \to \infty), \qquad \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta = \sum_n |c_n|^2 ,
 the second identity being Parseval’s. Perpendicularity is the easy half. Completeness, that no nonzero f is perpendicular to every e^{in\theta}, is the real content: trigonometric sums approximate every continuous periodic function uniformly (Fejér’s theorem), and continuous functions are dense in L^2 (Stein and Shakarchi, chapters 2 and 3).
At single points. Some continuous functions have Fourier series that diverge at a point, and Carleson proved in 1966 that the series of every L^2 function converges at almost every point. For shapes that are continuous and made of straight pieces it converges at every point (Dirichlet, 1829); the plucked triangle’s coefficients shrink like 1/n^2, which is why a few terms already look right in the demo below.


Build a plucked shape out of waves, then let it go:


  
  Waves used, up to
  Let goHear the loop, at the plucked point
  
  The loop is cut open and laid flat; its two edges are the same point. Dashed: the exact motion (once let go, the bump splits into two half-height copies that travel apart). Solid: the sum of the waves so far, each swinging at its own frequency. The sound adds those waves at the plucked point, the lowest at 196 Hz, faded only so that it stops.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
section: 2 · Why an equation that doesn’t change in time has modes
text:
2 · Why an equation that doesn’t change in time has modes
Why do such combinations exist? Three steps, for the two beads first.
1. The derivative of a solution is again a solution. Differentiate x'' = -Ax once in time. Because A doesn’t change with time, (x')'' = -A\,x': the velocity obeys the same equation. In pictures: a solution shifted in time, x(t + h), is a solution; by linearity so is (x(t + h) - x(t))/h, which becomes x' as h \to 0. Both ingredients matter: if A changed with time, differentiating would add -A'x, and the derivative of a nonlinear force on x is not the force on x'.
2. Look for a solution whose derivative is a multiple of itself, x' = s\,x for one number s. Then (e^{-st}x)' = 0, so x(t) = e^{st}X for a fixed column X.
3. Substitute. For x = e^{st}X, the equation x'' = -Ax reads s^2e^{st}X = -e^{st}AX, so 
A\,X = -s^2\,X :
 X is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue \lambda = -s^2. For the beads \lambda > 0, so s = \pm i\sqrt{\lambda} is imaginary, and by Euler’s formula, e^{i\omega t} = \cos\omega t + i\sin\omega t, the real part of e^{i\omega t}X is \cos(\omega t)\,X: the shape X swinging at angular frequency \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}. Two eigenvectors and two signs give four modes, as many as the numbers it takes to start two beads.
Every such equation, in one form. Collect the shape and its velocity into one state U = (u, u'). Then u'' = -Au becomes 
U' = B\,U, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I \\ -A & 0 \end{pmatrix},
 with I the identity (friction adds a term to the second row, section 4). Call B the equation’s generator: it turns the state into its rate of change. The same steps apply: U' is a solution whenever U is, and U = e^{st}W is one exactly when BW = sW.

Definition 1 (mode). For a linear system U' = BU with B constant: a nonzero solution U(t) = e^{st}W, i.e. BW = sW. If s is not real, its frequency is |\operatorname{Im} s|/2\pi and it fades at rate -\operatorname{Re} s; real motions are real parts, pairing s with its complex conjugate.

When \operatorname{Re} s < 0, the mode shrinks by the factor e in its fading time \tau = -1/\operatorname{Re} s. The swing of step 3 has its own, older name.

Definition 2 (normal mode). For u'' = -Au: a real solution u(t) = \cos(\omega t + \varphi)\,X with X \ne 0 and \omega > 0. It exists if and only if AX = \omega^2X.

How the two definitions meet. Write u'' = -Au as U' = BU with U = (u, u') and B as above. A normal mode with \omega > 0 is the real part of the pair of Definition-1 modes s = \pm i\omega, W = (X, \pm i\omega X). At \omega = 0 the pair collapses into a Jordan block, the smallest way for a matrix to lack eigenvectors (B sends (0, X) to (X, 0) and that to zero): the rigid drift X(a + bt), b \ne 0, is a solution but not a mode (a constant displacement X is an s = 0 mode). In finite dimensions B is diagonalizable, that is, has a basis of eigenvectors, exactly when A is diagonalizable and invertible.



ProofNormal modes, drifts, and when B has a basis of eigenvectors uses linear algebra

Definition 2’s condition. For u = \cos(\omega t + \varphi)X, u'' = -\omega^2\cos(\omega t + \varphi)X and -Au = -\cos(\omega t + \varphi)AX. These agree for all t if and only if AX = \omega^2X: if they agree, take a t with \cos(\omega t + \varphi) \ne 0 and divide; the converse is the computation itself.
Eigenvectors of B. Let W = (X, Y). Then BW = sW says Y = sX and -AX = sY, that is, W = (X, sX) with AX = -s^2X and X \neq 0. So each eigenvalue \lambda of A gives the eigenvalues s of B with s^2 = -\lambda: two of them, \pm\sqrt{-\lambda}, when \lambda \neq 0 (for \lambda = \omega^2 > 0, s = \pm i\omega), and only s = 0 when \lambda = 0. The eigenvectors of B for s are the (X, sX) with X in A’s eigenspace for \lambda = -s^2.
The real part of the pair. With W_\pm = (X, \pm i\omega X), \tfrac12\big(e^{i\varphi}e^{i\omega t}W_+ + e^{-i\varphi}e^{-i\omega t}W_-\big) = \big(\cos(\omega t + \varphi)X,\ -\omega\sin(\omega t + \varphi)X\big), which equals \operatorname{Re}\big(e^{i(\omega t + \varphi)}W_+\big) and is the state (u, u') of the normal mode.
The drift. If AX = 0 with X \ne 0, then B(X, 0) = (0, 0) and B(0, X) = (X, 0). The solution starting at (aX, bX) is (X(a + bt), bX), as differentiating checks. The only eigenvectors of B in the span of (X, 0) and (0, X) are the multiples of (X, 0), so for b \neq 0 this solution is not a combination of modes.
Counting. Work over the complex numbers, with A of size n, and let g_\lambda be the dimension of A’s eigenspace for \lambda. By the second paragraph, and since eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are independent, B, of size 2n, has exactly 2\sum_{\lambda\ne0} g_\lambda + g_0 independent eigenvectors. Since \sum_\lambda g_\lambda \le n, with equality exactly when A is diagonalizable, this is at most 2(n - g_0) + g_0 = 2n - g_0, and it equals 2n exactly when g_0 = 0 (A invertible) and \sum_\lambda g_\lambda = n (A diagonalizable).


How much this guarantees. In finite dimensions, at least one mode: BW = sW has a solution W \ne 0 exactly when the polynomial \det(B - s) (the determinant, a polynomial in s whose roots are the eigenvalues) vanishes, and every polynomial has a complex root. One mode is not a basis: x'' = 0 has only one (section 6). In infinite dimensions there may be none: on an infinite string the solutions e^{\pm ikx} of -c^2X'' = \lambda X have infinite energy, so none is an allowed shape.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
3 · The criterion
When are the modes enough for every motion? In words (precise statement and proof in the fold):

The criterion. The solutions of an equation are exactly all combinations of a fixed set of modes, with any amounts, when and only when the equation is linear, unchanging in time, and its generator has a full set of eigenvectors.

Checked on the two beads. Their A has the eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1) with the positive eigenvalues \lambda_1 = T/mh and \lambda_2 = 3T/mh, so it is diagonalizable and invertible, and B has the full set of four eigenvectors (X, \pm i\omega X), for s = \pm i\omega_1, \pm i\omega_2. So the solutions are exactly the combinations of these four modes with any amounts; in real form, 
x(t) = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\big(a_1\cos\omega_1 t + b_1\sin\omega_1 t\big) + \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\big(a_2\cos\omega_2 t + b_2\sin\omega_2 t\big), \qquad \omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k},
 with any four real numbers, which the starting heights and velocities fix. On the two-bead ring the criterion fails: A_{\text{ring}} has the eigenvalue 0, so B has only three independent eigenvectors, and the drift (1, 1)(a + bt), b \neq 0, is a solution no combination of modes produces. Split it off, as the takeaway does, and the rest passes.

Definition 3 (modal system). One whose modes form a basis of its states: every state is uniquely a (convergent) combination of mode vectors. (Infinite dimensions: a Riesz basis of the energy space, not merely a complete set.)

The two tied beads are modal; the two-bead ring is not. Section 5 explains the Riesz basis.



ProofThe criterion as an equality of sets uses linear algebra

Statement. Let F: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^n, and call a differentiable U: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}^n a solution of U' = F(U) if U'(t) = F(U(t)) for every t. Let W_1, \dots, W_n be a basis of \mathbb{C}^n, let s_1, \dots, s_n be complex numbers, and let W be the matrix with columns W_k. Then the solutions of U' = F(U) are exactly all combinations 
U(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n c_k\,e^{s_k t}\,W_k ,
 with every coefficient vector c = (c_1, \dots, c_n) \in \mathbb{C}^n allowed, if and only if F(U) = BU for every U, with B = W\operatorname{diag}(s)\,W^{-1}.
Proof of “if”. Suppose F(U) = BU with B = W\operatorname{diag}(s)W^{-1}. Then BW = W\operatorname{diag}(s), which says BW_k = s_kW_k for each k. For any c, the function U(t) = \sum_k c_ke^{s_kt}W_k has U'(t) = \sum_k c_ks_ke^{s_kt}W_k = \sum_k c_ke^{s_kt}BW_k = BU(t), so it is a solution. Conversely, let U be any solution, and set c = W^{-1}U(0) and V(t) = \sum_k c_ke^{s_kt}W_k, a solution with V(0) = U(0). The difference Z = W^{-1}(U - V) satisfies Z' = W^{-1}B(U - V) = \operatorname{diag}(s)Z, so each entry obeys z_k' = s_kz_k; then (e^{-s_kt}z_k)' = 0, so z_k(t) = e^{s_kt}z_k(0) = 0. Hence U = V.
Proof of “only if”. Suppose the solutions are exactly the combinations, every c allowed. Take any vector Y \in \mathbb{C}^n and choose c = W^{-1}Y, which is allowed. The solution U(t) = \sum_kc_ke^{s_kt}W_k has U(0) = Wc = Y and U'(0) = \sum_kc_ks_kW_k = W\operatorname{diag}(s)\,c = W\operatorname{diag}(s)W^{-1}Y. Because U is a solution, U'(0) = F(U(0)) = F(Y). So F(Y) = W\operatorname{diag}(s)W^{-1}Y for every Y: the equation at time 0, applied to solutions starting at every state, forces F to be this linear map.
Remarks. (1) The same argument at any time t_0 in place of 0 shows that even an equation allowed to change in time, U' = F(t, U), whose solutions are exactly these combinations must have F(t, U) = BU for every t: linearity and time-invariance both follow, as the criterion in words says. (2) For a real equation, such as u'' = -Au with A real, the real solutions are those whose coefficients pair each mode with its complex conjugate, c_k with \bar c_k. (3) For continuous objects the same holds with a Riesz basis of the energy space in place of a basis, and square-summable coefficients (section 5).





PreciselyWhy “with any amounts” matters uses derivatives

Exponentials with fixed exponents alone do not force an equation to be linear. On the half-line U > -\tfrac14, take 
U' = 2U - \frac{\sqrt{1 + 4U} - 1}{2} ,
 whose right side is smooth there. Every solution is 
U(t) = c\,e^{t} + c^2\,e^{2t}
 for one real number c, for as long as it stays in U > -\tfrac14: for c \ge 0 that is all t, and for c < 0 the solution reaches the edge U = -\tfrac14 when c\,e^t = -\tfrac12.
Proof. Put w = (\sqrt{1 + 4U} - 1)/2, which maps U > -\tfrac14 one-to-one onto w > -\tfrac12, with inverse U = w^2 + w. In terms of w the equation reads (2w + 1)\,w' = 2(w^2 + w) - w = w\,(2w + 1). Since 2w + 1 > 0, this is w' = w, so w = c\,e^t, and U = w^2 + w = c\,e^t + c^2e^{2t}, valid while c\,e^t > -\tfrac12.
Every solution is built from the same two exponentials, e^t and e^{2t}, yet the equation is not linear: the coefficients are tied, the second always the square of the first, and the sum of two solutions, (c + d)e^t + (c^2 + d^2)e^{2t}, is not a solution unless cd = 0. In the criterion, “every coefficient vector allowed” rules this out.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
section: 4 · Three levels, from the familiar to the general
text:
4 · Three levels, from the familiar to the general
Three nested classes of equations, each with its exact condition: level 1 gives pure tones, level 2 adds fading, level 3 adds shapes whose parts lag behind one another.

Level 1 · Free vibration without friction
The equation is u'' = -Au with A self-adjoint and positive: pure tones at \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi, energy conserved. For beads, self-adjoint means symmetric, entry (i, j) equal to entry (j, i), and positive, A > 0, means x\cdot Ax > 0 for every x \ne 0.

Result (level 1, any number of beads). Let A be a real symmetric n\times n matrix with A > 0.

A has eigenvectors X_1, \dots, X_n forming an orthonormal basis (perpendicular, each of length 1), with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n > 0.
Every solution of x'' = -Ax is 
x(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\Big(a_i\cos\omega_i t + \frac{b_i}{\omega_i}\sin\omega_i t\Big), \qquad \omega_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i},
 with a_i = X_i\cdot x(0) and b_i = X_i\cdot x'(0): mode i sounds at f_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}/2\pi.
The energy E = \tfrac12\,x'\cdot x' + \tfrac12\,x\cdot Ax is the same at every moment.





ProofLevel 1 for any number of beads, and where symmetry comes from uses linear algebra

Part 1 is the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices; \lambda_i = X_i\cdot AX_i > 0 because A > 0.
For part 2, write x(t) = \sum_j c_j(t)X_j with c_j = X_j\cdot x, the amount of X_j in x. Take the dot product of x'' = -Ax with X_i. On the left, X_i\cdot x'' = c_i''. On the right, X_i\cdot Ax = (AX_i)\cdot x, because both sides equal \sum_{j,k}(X_i)_jA_{jk}x_k once A_{jk} = A_{kj}; so X_i\cdot Ax = \lambda_iX_i\cdot x = \lambda_ic_i. Hence c_i'' = -\lambda_ic_i for each i separately: n independent springs. Each has exactly one solution with c_i(0) = a_i and c_i'(0) = b_i, namely a_i\cos\omega_it + (b_i/\omega_i)\sin\omega_it (uniqueness as in the criterion’s proof).
For part 3, E' = x'\cdot x'' + \tfrac12(x'\cdot Ax + x\cdot Ax') = x'\cdot(x'' + Ax) = 0, using x\cdot Ax' = x'\cdot Ax for symmetric A.
Drifts. If A is symmetric with A \ge 0 and has the eigenvalue 0, its eigenvectors for 0 (the drifts) are perpendicular to the others, and A maps the perpendicular complement of the drifts to itself and is positive there. The motion splits accordingly: along each drift X, c'' = 0, so c = a + bt; on the rest, the result above.
Symmetry from energy. Near rest the stored energy is V(x) \approx \tfrac12\,x\cdot Kx, where the stiffness matrix K is the matrix of second derivatives of V, symmetric because mixed partial derivatives don’t depend on the order of differentiation. The restoring force is -\nabla V \approx -Kx, keeping the first-order term; that is where linearity comes from. A stable rest means x\cdot Kx > 0 except along rigid drifts.
Unequal masses. Newton’s law reads Mx'' = -Kx with M the diagonal matrix of masses, and A = M^{-1}K is symmetric in the mass-weighted dot product \sum_i m_ix_iy_i; equivalently v = M^{1/2}x obeys v'' = -M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}v with a symmetric matrix.


Why the instruments qualify. Symmetry: a stretch of string feels only the difference of its two beads’ heights, so bead j pulls bead i as hard as i pulls j. Positivity: displacing a held object stores energy. A shape storing none is a rigid drift, \lambda = 0, moving as X(a + bt); it is split off. For strings, tubes, bars and drums, with \langle f, g\rangle = \int f\,g, integration by parts gives symmetry and positivity (fold); that every shape is a sum of modes needs finiteness (section 5).



ProofSymmetry and energy for strings, bars and drums uses integration by parts

For the string with tied ends, integrate by parts once: 
\langle Af, g\rangle = -c^2\int_0^L f''\,g\,dx = -c^2\big[f'\,g\big]_0^L + c^2\int_0^L f'\,g'\,dx = c^2\int_0^L f'\,g'\,dx ,
 since g(0) = g(L) = 0. The last expression does not change when f and g swap, so \langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle, and with g = f it is c^2\int (f')^2 \ge 0, zero only for a constant shape, which a tied end forbids. The bracket also vanishes on a loop and at a closed tube end, where f' = 0. For a bar, integrating by parts twice gives \kappa^2\int f''g''\,dx, every boundary term killed by clamped, pinned or free ends; for a drumhead, the two-dimensional version gives c^2\iint\nabla f\cdot\nabla g\,dA, the rim term killed by the fixed rim.
Two consequences follow as for matrices. Modes with different eigenvalues are perpendicular: if AX = \lambda X and AY = \mu Y, then \lambda\langle X, Y\rangle = \langle AX, Y\rangle = \langle X, AY\rangle = \mu\langle X, Y\rangle. And energy is conserved: with E = \tfrac12\langle u_t, u_t\rangle + \tfrac12\langle Au, u\rangle, symmetry gives E' = \langle u_t, u_{tt} + Au\rangle = 0; times the mass per unit length, the two terms are the kinetic energy and the energy stored in the stretched string, \tfrac12T\int u_x^2\,dx.




Level 2 · Friction that the same shapes split
The equation is 
u'' + C\,u' + A\,u = 0 ,
 with the friction C symmetric and commuting with A: AC = CA, that is, applying C then A gives the same as A then C. For example C = \alpha + \beta A (numbers \alpha, \beta; \alpha stands for \alpha I). In general, for unequal masses, Mu'' + Cu' + Ku = 0, the condition is CM^{-1}K = KM^{-1}C (Caughey and O’Kelly 1965). The standing shapes stay real, and each fades.

Result (level 2). Let A and C be real symmetric n\times n matrices with AC = CA.

There is an orthonormal basis X_1, \dots, X_n of shared eigenvectors: AX_k = \lambda_kX_k and CX_k = \gamma_kX_k.
Every solution of u'' + Cu' + Au = 0 is u(t) = \sum_k q_k(t)X_k, where each amount obeys its own equation, q_k'' + \gamma_kq_k' + \lambda_kq_k = 0.
The system is modal exactly when, for every shared eigenvector (with values \lambda for A and \gamma for C), s^2 + \gamma s + \lambda = 0 has distinct roots.

For light friction, \gamma_k^2 < 4\lambda_k, mode k is the real shape X_k swinging at f_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k - \gamma_k^2/4}\,/2\pi and fading with the time \tau_k = 2/\gamma_k.

Critical damping of one mode, \gamma^2 = 4\lambda, breaks it: the roots coincide, and that mode moves as (a + bt)e^{-\gamma t/2}, which no combination of modes produces (section 6).



ProofLevel 2 uses linear algebra

Part 1. Each eigenspace E_\lambda of A is mapped to itself by C: if AX = \lambda X then A(CX) = CAX = \lambda\,CX. On E_\lambda, C is symmetric, so E_\lambda has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of C. Together over all \lambda these give part 1, since the eigenspaces of A are perpendicular and fill out \mathbb{R}^n.
Part 2. Take the dot product of the equation with X_k and use symmetry as in level 1: X_k\cdot Cu' = \gamma_kq_k' and X_k\cdot Au = \lambda_kq_k, with q_k = X_k\cdot u.
Part 3. In the state U = (u, u') the generator is B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & I \\ -A & -C\end{smallmatrix}\right). In the basis (X_1, 0), (0, X_1), \dots, (X_n, 0), (0, X_n) it splits into 2\times2 blocks B_k = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\lambda_k & -\gamma_k\end{smallmatrix}\right), with characteristic polynomial s^2 + \gamma_ks + \lambda_k. A 2\times2 matrix with two distinct eigenvalues has two independent eigenvectors. If the eigenvalue s_0 is repeated, B_k - s_0 is not zero (its top right entry is 1), so it has rank 1 and B_k has only one eigenvector: a Jordan block. B has a basis of eigenvectors exactly when every block does.
Light friction. For \gamma_k^2 < 4\lambda_k the roots are s = -\gamma_k/2 \pm i\sqrt{\lambda_k - \gamma_k^2/4}, and the real solutions are q_k = e^{-\gamma_kt/2}\big(a\cos\tilde\omega_kt + b\sin\tilde\omega_kt\big) with \tilde\omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k - \gamma_k^2/4}.
Why C must be symmetric. Friction that turns motion into heat comes from a dissipation function \tfrac12\,u'\cdot Cu', as Rayleigh introduced it, and is symmetric. An antisymmetric velocity term, such as a spinning object’s gyroscopic force, does no work and can commute with A (for A = \omega^2I it commutes with everything), yet its modes are rotating motions with complex shapes such as (1, \pm i), not real standing shapes.


Two piano strings in tune. A piano note has two or three strings tuned alike on one bridge. Keep one mode per string, one number q_j each; in tune, A = \omega_0^2I on the pair. The bridge, driven by both strings at once, gives each a friction in proportion to its motion: C = r\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right), symmetric (the strings’ own losses aside). A multiple of the identity commutes with every matrix: level 2. The shared eigenvectors are (1, 1), swinging together, with \gamma = 2r: both push the yielding bridge, and the mode fades at the rate \gamma/2 = r; and (1, -1), swinging oppositely, with \gamma = 0: their pushes cancel. An even hammer starts only (1, 1); an unequal strike starts both, so each string’s motion decays in two stages, fast then slow, in real modes, exactly in or out of step. This is the first half of Weinreich’s (1977) explanation: in this exact model the slow mode does not push the bridge at all, so it would hardly be heard; he showed that the strings’ slight mistuning, together with the hammer’s small irregularities, governs the aftersound, which is level 3.


Level 3 · The general case
The equation is any U' = BU. With a basis of eigenvectors it is modal, its modes in general complex: the entries of W have different phases, so parts of the shape peak at different moments.
The same two strings, mistuned. With A = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_1^2, \omega_2^2), \omega_1 \ne \omega_2, A no longer commutes with C. For a mistuning \delta = \omega_1 - \omega_2 about as large as r the modes are strongly complex: in each the strings swing out of step by an angle other than 0^\circ or 180^\circ, and both modes push the bridge, so the slow one is heard: the aftersound (numbers in the fold).
Radiation lands here too. Sound carried into unbounded air is a loss that depends on the shape and frequency, and the problem is no longer self-adjoint.



DetailsThe two strings, in tune and mistuned, in numbers uses complex numbers

This is a toy model: each string reduced to one mode, the bridge to the friction C = r\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right), and the strings’ own losses left out. For light friction and small mistuning, write u = \operatorname{Re}\big(a(t)\,e^{i\bar\omega t}\big) with \bar\omega = (\omega_1 + \omega_2)/2 and a slowly changing complex column a. Keeping first-order terms in r and \delta, the equation becomes 
a' = M a, \qquad M = \begin{pmatrix} i\delta/2 - r/2 & -r/2 \\ -r/2 & -i\delta/2 - r/2\end{pmatrix} ,
 with eigenvalues -\tfrac r2 \pm \tfrac12\sqrt{r^2 - \delta^2}.

In tune, \delta = 0: eigenvalues 0 and -r, eigenvectors (1, -1) and (1, 1), real.
Mistuned by less than r (at \delta = 0.6\,r: the strings swing equally far in each mode, 37^\circ apart in the nearly-together mode, fading at 0.9\,r, and 143^\circ apart in the nearly-opposite one, fading at 0.1\,r): both modes at one frequency, fading at the different rates \tfrac r2 \mp \tfrac12\sqrt{r^2 - \delta^2}. The eigenvector ratio a_2/a_1 = (i\delta/2 \mp \tfrac12\sqrt{r^2 - \delta^2})\cdot 2/r has modulus 1 and a phase other than 0 and 180^\circ. For \delta = 0.6\,r: rates 0.1\,r and 0.9\,r, ratios -0.8 + 0.6i and 0.8 + 0.6i, phases 143^\circ and 37^\circ.
Mistuned by exactly r: the two eigenvalues coincide at -r/2 with the single eigenvector (1, i), a Jordan block.
Mistuned by more than r: the frequencies split by \sqrt{\delta^2 - r^2} and both modes fade at the rate r/2: the strings beat.

A numerical check of the full equations u'' + Cu' + Au = 0, with r at 2% of \omega_0 and \delta = 0.6\,r, gives the same phases to within 0.01^\circ.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
5 · The deeper theory
This section needs linear algebra and analysis. Skip to section 6 if you prefer; sections 6 and 7 can be read without it.
Self-adjoint A \ge 0: the spectral theorem. On a Hilbert space of shapes (with an inner product, and limits), von Neumann’s spectral theorem (1930, 1932) represents A as multiplication by \lambda on its spectral parts, which defines \varphi(A): multiply the part at \lambda by \varphi(\lambda). This always expresses the solution through A’s spectrum, 
u(t) = \cos\!\big(t\sqrt{A}\big)\,f + \frac{\sin\!\big(t\sqrt{A}\big)}{\sqrt{A}}\,g ,
 for starting shape f and velocity g, reading \sin(t\sqrt A)/\sqrt A as t on drifts. For a matrix, \cos(t\sqrt A)f = \sum_i\cos(t\sqrt{\lambda_i})\,(X_i\cdot f)\,X_i: level 1’s formula. The spectrum is the set of numbers z for which A - z has no bounded inverse; for self-adjoint A \ge 0 it lies in [0, \infty).
A list of notes exactly when the resolvent is compact. The resolvent (A - z)^{-1} solves Au - zu = f for u. An operator is compact if it maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure; on a Hilbert space, equivalently, it is a limit in norm of operators with finite-dimensional range. For self-adjoint A \ge 0, (A + 1)^{-1} is compact exactly when the spectrum is a discrete list, eigenvalues \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty of finite multiplicity, with eigenvectors forming an orthonormal basis (fold). Then the formula is a sum over modes, a list of notes, and with A > 0 the modes of B form an orthonormal basis of the energy space, the states (u, u') of finite energy. In finite dimensions every operator is compact; for continuous objects, this is what “the object is finite” means.
Which objects have it. Strings and tubes, by Sturm–Liouville theory; bars, by the same theorem through a compact Green’s operator; drums on a bounded region with a reasonable edge, by Rellich’s theorem (fold). Courant and Hilbert (volume 1, chapters V and VI) treat all of these. Which shapes share a list of notes: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
The infinite string: spectral, but no list of notes. On the whole line A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 is self-adjoint and \ge 0 with spectrum [0, \infty) and no eigenvectors; the resolvent is not compact. The formula still holds, the sum over modes becoming the Fourier transform, 
u(x, t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Big(\hat f(k)\cos(ckt) + \hat g(k)\,\frac{\sin(ckt)}{ck}\Big)e^{ikx}\,dk ,
 a continuous spread of frequencies.
Without symmetry (friction, radiation), for losses that only remove energy, the motion still exists and is unique (a semigroup), but the eigenvectors may fail to form a basis, and whether they form a Riesz basis has to be proved case by case (Gohberg and Krein). For a string with friction varying along it they do (Cox and Zuazua), and decaying modes can still make the motion grow for a while (Trefethen and Embree). Details in the fold.
Nonlinear or time-dependent equations have no spectrum in this sense: by the criterion, their solutions are not all the combinations of a fixed set of modes.



PreciselyWhich objects have a compact resolvent, and solutions in the energy sense uses functional analysis


Strings and tubes: Sturm–Liouville theory. On a finite interval, -(pu')' + qu = \lambda\rho u with p, \rho > 0 and a condition at each end has simple eigenvalues \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \cdots \to \infty and eigenfunctions forming an orthogonal basis.
Bars: the same theorem through a compact Green’s operator. The fourth-order bar is not a classical Sturm–Liouville problem, but (A + 1)^{-1} is f \mapsto \int G(x, y)f(y)\,dy with a kernel G, the Green’s function, continuous on the square [0, L]^2, which makes it compact.
Drums: Rellich’s theorem, on a bounded region with a reasonable edge: any set of shapes whose energies \iint(|\nabla u|^2 + u^2) are bounded by one number has compact closure in L^2, so the resolvent is compact. For a head fixed at its rim any bounded region will do; with a free edge, very irregular regions can fail.

Solutions in the energy sense. For a start of finite energy the formula gives the one motion of finite energy, which conserves it. A plucked string’s kink has no second derivative, so the plucked string solves u_{tt} = -Au in this sense, not point by point.





ProofA list of notes exactly when the resolvent is compact uses functional analysis

Let A \ge 0 be self-adjoint on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H. Claim: R = (A + 1)^{-1} is compact if and only if H has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors X_k of A whose eigenvalues \lambda_k have finite multiplicity and tend to \infty.
If R is compact. R is bounded, with \|R\| \le 1 because \langle(A + 1)u, u\rangle \ge \|u\|^2; it is self-adjoint; and it is one-to-one, having the inverse A + 1. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators gives an orthonormal basis of the closure of its range, which is H because R is self-adjoint and one-to-one, made of eigenvectors RX_k = \mu_kX_k with \mu_k \to 0, each nonzero \mu_k of finite multiplicity, and no \mu_k = 0. Applying A + 1 gives X_k = \mu_k(A + 1)X_k, so AX_k = \lambda_kX_k with \lambda_k = 1/\mu_k - 1 \to \infty.
If such a basis exists. List the \lambda_k in increasing order. Then Rf = \sum_k(1 + \lambda_k)^{-1}\langle f, X_k\rangle X_k. Its truncations R_N, summing over k \le N, have finite-dimensional range, and \|R - R_N\| = \sup_{k > N}(1 + \lambda_k)^{-1} \to 0. A limit in norm of such operators is compact.
The energy space. Measure the energy of a state by \|(u, v)\|_E^2 = \langle Au, u\rangle + \langle v, v\rangle. For A > 0 with such a basis, the states W_{k,\pm} = (X_k, \pm i\omega_kX_k)/\sqrt{2\lambda_k}, \omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k}, have \|W_{k,\pm}\|_E^2 = (\lambda_k + \omega_k^2)/2\lambda_k = 1, are mutually perpendicular (for the pair, \lambda_k + (i\omega_k)\overline{(-i\omega_k)} = \lambda_k - \omega_k^2 = 0), and span the energy space; so they form an orthonormal basis of it, and the system is modal in the sense of Definition 3.





PreciselyWithout symmetry: semigroups, Riesz bases and growth before decay uses functional analysis

Semigroups. For a damped string or drum, energy can only decrease, \operatorname{Re}\langle BU, U\rangle_E \le 0 in the energy inner product, and B generates a contraction semigroup e^{tB}: bounded operators with e^{(t + t')B} = e^{tB}e^{t'B}, e^{0B} = I, continuous in t, sending the starting state to the state at time t, provided also that 1 - B is onto (together: B is maximally dissipative; the Lumer–Phillips theorem). This gives existence and uniqueness without any modes.
Riesz bases. In finite dimensions the only way to lack a basis of eigenvectors is a Jordan block. In infinite dimensions the eigenvectors can be complete (no state is perpendicular to all of them) and still not be a basis, or be a basis in which expansions are unstable. The property that makes mode expansions behave like orthonormal ones is a Riesz basis: the image of an orthonormal basis under a bounded operator with a bounded inverse; equivalently, every state is uniquely U = \sum_kc_kW_k with m\sum_k|c_k|^2 \le \|U\|^2 \le M\sum_k|c_k|^2 for fixed 0 < m \le M. Gohberg and Krein (1969) is the classical account of when the eigenvectors of a non-self-adjoint operator are complete or form a basis. For the string u_{tt} + 2a(x)\,u_t = u_{xx} on a finite interval, ends tied, with a friction coefficient a of bounded variation, Cox and Zuazua (1994) proved that the eigenvectors form a Riesz basis of the energy space, and that the energy decays at exactly the rate set by the slowest-fading mode.
Growth before decay. Even with a basis of decaying modes, a non-normal B, one that does not commute with its adjoint, so that its eigenvectors are not perpendicular, can make the size of the state grow for a while. The smallest example: B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 10 \\ 0 & -2\end{smallmatrix}\right) has modes fading at the rates 1 and 2, with the nearly parallel eigenvectors (1, 0) and (-10, 1). Starting from U(0) = (0, 1) = 10\,(1, 0) + (-10, 1), a near cancellation of two large modes, 
U(t) = \big(10\,(e^{-t} - e^{-2t}),\ e^{-2t}\big),
 which reaches size about 2.5 near t = 0.7 before it decays: the two modes fade at different rates and stop cancelling. Pseudospectra, the sets of z where \|(B - z)^{-1}\| is large, measure this (Trefethen and Embree 2005).
Radiation. For an object radiating into unbounded air, the slowly fading “modes” are resonances: complex frequencies at which the resolvent, continued past the real axis, has poles. Expansions in them hold only in restricted senses.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
6 · Counterexamples, smallest first
1. A drift: x'' = 0. The generator B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\right) has only the eigenvalue 0 and only the eigenvectors along (1, 0), so x = a + bt with b \ne 0 is not a combination of modes: a Jordan block. You hear nothing. In instruments: the two-bead ring, a free bar or drum sliding as a whole; split off.
2. Critical damping: u'' + 2u' + u = 0. The roots of s^2 + 2s + 1 = (s + 1)^2 coincide, B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\-1 & -2\end{smallmatrix}\right) has the single eigenvector (1, -1), and the solutions are (a + bt)\,e^{-t}: the same Jordan block, moved by friction. You hear no ring: released, the mass creeps back to rest without swinging.
3. A property that changes in time. In Mathieu’s equation x'' = -(1 + \varepsilon\cos 2t)\,x the stiffness wobbles, and differentiating a solution adds the term 2\varepsilon\sin(2t)\,x: no modes e^{st}W. By Floquet’s theorem the solutions are combinations of e^{\mu t}p(t) with p periodic, and for every small \varepsilon \neq 0 one exponent has a positive real part, about \varepsilon/4: parametric resonance, as when a child pumps a swing. A slow change is gentler: a talking drum’s player squeezes its cords while it rings, and when the tension changes slowly compared with one swing, each mode keeps its shape and its frequency follows the tension, to a good approximation. You hear the pitch glide with the squeeze, even within one stroke.
4. A force not proportional to the displacement. The wide pendulum, x'' = -\sin x, is nonlinear and softening: wider swings are slower. Strings and drumheads stiffen instead, so a loud stroke starts sharp and its pitch drops as it fades. You hear pitch that moves with loudness: a hard guitar pluck’s twang, a gong’s glide; and a tamtam’s shimmer builds up as energy moves into higher modes (fold).



DetailsSoftening, stiffening, and what you hear uses no extra mathematics

The pendulum swung wide, x'' = -\sin x, is nonlinear (\sin 2x \neq 2\sin x, so twice a solution is not one) and softening: its force grows less than in proportion, so wider swings are slower; out to 90^\circ a swing takes 18% longer than a small one. Strings and drumheads go the other way: a wide swing stretches them and raises the average tension, so a loud stroke starts sharp and its pitch drops as it fades. You hear a hard guitar pluck’s twang; the slight pitch drop of a loud kettledrum stroke; a gong’s pitch glide, up for some gongs and down for others, depending on the shell’s curvature and thickness; and a tamtam’s or cymbal’s shimmer building up after the strike, as the nonlinearity passes energy from low modes into high ones. In a modal system each mode’s amount evolves on its own, so energy cannot flow between modes.


5. Rayleigh’s self-sustained oscillator. In Rayleigh’s equation (1883), 
x'' - \varepsilon\,\big(x' - \tfrac13 x'^3\big) + x = 0 ,
 the middle term feeds energy in when the motion is slow and takes it out when it is fast. Every motion except rest settles into one repeating cycle, a limit cycle, of amplitude about 2 and angular frequency 1 - \varepsilon^2/16 + \cdots, near the linear value 1. It has no modes; being periodic, its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples. You hear the steady tone of a bowed string, a reed or a player’s lips, exactly harmonic for as long as the player keeps going; and a harmonica’s bent notes, where the player’s mouth, with the hole’s other reed, pulls the playing frequency.
6. The infinite string. On the whole line, u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} is linear, unchanging in time, symmetric and positive, with no allowed eigenvectors: spectral (section 5), no list of notes. You hear a click: a pluck splits into two half-height bumps that run apart, and each point falls still once they have passed.

The counterexamples, smallest first.







Counterexample
What fails
What you hear




1 drift

3 pumped swing; talking drum
