PreciselyThe counterexamples in equations uses differential equations

Stability. An unstable rest, x'' = +x (A = -1), is modal, with the real exponents s = \pm1, but one mode runs away exponentially: the takeaway’s “stable” is A \ge 0, and after any drifts (\lambda = 0) are split off, A > 0.
The pumped swing. For x'' + (1 + \varepsilon\cos 2t)x = 0 the map from the state at time 0 to the state at time \pi is a fixed matrix P (the coefficient has period \pi). Floquet’s theorem (1883) writes every solution, when P has two distinct eigenvalues as here, as a combination of e^{\mu t}p(t) with p of period \pi and e^{\mu\pi} an eigenvalue of P (\mu may be complex). A numerical computation of P gives the growth rate \operatorname{Re}\mu = 0.0125, 0.0250, 0.0499 for \varepsilon = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2: about \varepsilon/4.
The slow change. For x'' + \omega(t)^2x = 0 with \omega changing slowly compared with one swing, x \approx (a/\sqrt{\omega(t)})\cos\big(\int_0^t\omega\,dt' + \varphi\big): the frequency follows \omega(t), and the energy divided by the frequency stays nearly constant (an adiabatic invariant).
The wide pendulum. The period of x'' = -\sin x with amplitude x_0 is 4K(\sin^2(x_0/2)), where K(m) = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - m\sin^2\phi)^{-1/2}\,d\phi, against 2\pi for small swings; at x_0 = 90^\circ the ratio is 1.180.
Rayleigh’s oscillator. A numerical run of x'' - \varepsilon(x' - x'^3/3) + x = 0 settles to angular frequency 0.99938, 0.9944, 0.9847 for \varepsilon = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, against 1 - \varepsilon^2/16 = 0.99938, 0.99438, 0.98438, with amplitude about 2. By contrast, a linear system driven by a periodic force is solved by its modes, and without friction the response at an exact resonance grows in proportion to time.
Spinning objects. Gyroscopic forces Gu' with G antisymmetric do no work and need no friction, yet the equation is not of the form Mu'' = -Ku: the classical theory of small oscillations covers “natural” mechanical systems, whose energy is kinetic plus stored, without such terms.
The surrounding air. Treated as not squeezable near a drumhead, the air adds a fixed, symmetric, positive added mass, a generalized eigenvalue problem AX = \omega^2(1 + M_{\text{air}}/\sigma)X inside level 1 once lengths are measured with the masses as weights, \langle x, (\sigma + M_{\text{air}})y\rangle, as in the unequal-masses fold. Exactly, the added mass depends on the frequency and is complex, because sound radiates away into unbounded air, and the modes become resonances that fade at the rate the head radiates energy.
No edges. On the whole line, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 has the continuous spectrum [0, \infty) and no eigenfunctions with finite \int|X|^2. With u_t(x, 0) = 0, d’Alembert’s solution u(x, t) = \tfrac12\big(f(x - ct) + f(x + ct)\big) shows the two half-height bumps; once both have passed a point, the string there is at rest.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
7 · Back to what you hear
The motion is not yet the sound. Between the object and your ear sit the instrument’s body (a violin’s box, a piano’s soundboard), the air and the room, and each is a linear filter that doesn’t change in time; for a room this holds very well at the pressures of music, as long as nothing in it moves (Masovic). Such a filter keeps every f_k and \tau_k, changes the amounts a_k and phases \varphi_k, and adds its own ringing: the body’s resonances, and the room’s reverberation, which goes on after the instrument’s modes have faded and is how a room lengthens what you hear. The reason is section 2’s again: a filter that is the same at every moment sends e^{st} to a multiple of e^{st}, plus terms at its own exponents (fold). So the instrument’s part of the sound is 
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\,e^{-t/\tau_k}\cos(2\pi f_kt + \varphi_k) ,
 one term per mode, s = -1/\tau_k \pm 2\pi i f_k. The equation of motion (the operator, together with friction and radiation) fixes the f_k and \tau_k; the playing, the radiation and where you listen fix the a_k. The series derives the f_k; the \tau_k are mostly measured, and it says so where it uses them.



ProofA filter keeps every exponent and adds its own uses integrals

A linear filter that is the same at every moment, at rest before the input v starts at t = 0, has output p(t) = \int_0^t h(t - t')\,v(t')\,dt', where h is its response to a sudden tap. Take a body with finitely many decaying resonances, h(t) = \sum_jb_je^{r_jt} with \operatorname{Re} r_j < 0, and the input v(t) = e^{st} with s different from every r_j. Then 
p(t) = \sum_j b_je^{r_jt}\int_0^te^{(s - r_j)t'}\,dt' = H(s)\,e^{st} - \sum_j\frac{b_j}{s - r_j}\,e^{r_jt}, \qquad H(s) = \sum_j\frac{b_j}{s - r_j} .
 The input’s exponent s, and with it its frequency and fading time, comes out unchanged, multiplied by the number H(s): its size scaled by |H(s)| and its phase shifted by the angle of H(s). The other terms are the filter’s own ringing, at its own exponents r_j. By linearity a sum of modes passes term by term, and a real input, the sum of a mode and its conjugate, gives a real output. A propagation delay d multiplies e^{st} by e^{-sd}, again the same exponent.


The four aspects of sound, from the three lists. Post 1 defines pitch, loudness, timbre and duration as things we hear. What each is heard from, through the ear’s own weighting, is a fact about hearing, from psychoacoustics, not mathematics:

The four aspects (Moore 2012; ISO 226; Stevens 1957).







Aspect
Heard from
Set by




Pitch
mainly where the f_k sit: for a single tone whose prominent partials lie near a harmonic series in the pitch range, that series’ base
the equation of motion


Loudness
the sizes a_k, weighted by frequency (equal-loudness contours); about twice as loud per 10 dB
the playing, the radiation, where you listen


Timbre
all three lists, f_k, a_k and \tau_k, especially early on, plus noise that is not a mode
all of these


Duration
the fading times \tau_k, and when the player stops or damps the note
friction and radiation, and the player



Bowed and blown instruments are different: their motion is a single repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples; the resonator’s modes shape which partials are strong, and the player sets loudness and duration.
The four routes to a clear pitch, now explained. Post 1 lists four ways to partials at or very near whole-number multiples of one frequency. Each is a statement about these lists.

By nature: strings and air columns. On an interval with tied or open ends, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 gives f_n = nc/2L, for section 1’s two reasons; a tube closed at one end, like a clarinet’s, gives the odd multiples (2n - 1)c/4L.
By design. Added stiffness never lowers an eigenvalue and added mass never raises one (the min–max principle), so makers reshape the operator until the modes that matter land near the lines: a kettledrum’s air loading, a marimba bar’s undercut, the tabla’s loaded patch, a bell’s profile (most principal partials on a harmonic series; the tierce, a minor third above the prime, is not on the series).
By suppression. A short \tau_k, like a kalimba tine’s fast-dying off-line overtone, or a small a_k and short \tau_k together, like a kettledrum’s off-line round modes, which the usual playing spot starts more weakly than the spoke modes (drum page) and which radiate their energy away fast (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 18; Packer 1993).
By a periodic drive: bow and breath. Section 6’s Rayleigh oscillator: a limit cycle, exactly periodic and so exactly harmonic.

title: When an equation has a spectrum
text:
What we found
An equation’s solutions are exactly all the combinations of its modes, with any amounts, when it is linear, unchanging in time, and its generator has a basis of eigenvectors. The free vibration of a stable, frictionless, finite object always passes, at \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi; friction that the same shapes split keeps it, short of critical damping; general friction and radiation give complex modes, whose basis has to be proved. Each failure has a smallest example, and most can be heard.

title: Instruments, case by case
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 3 · When an equation has a spectrum · Violin → · Glossary
The question. For a particular instrument, what decides how it sounds: where its partials can sit, how it is played, or how its sound fades?
The series in one paragraph

title: Instruments, case by case
section: Three things that decide a sound
text:
Three things that decide a sound
Each page asks which of three things decides how an instrument sounds: its spectrum, the frequencies its operator allows, which says where partials can sit; the playing, which says which modes start and how strongly; and the fading, which includes the player’s damping; a bowed or blown instrument instead runs one repeating cycle, whose partials sit on whole-number multiples and are shaped by its resonator’s modes (the series in one paragraph).

title: Instruments, case by case
text:
The orchestra
Musicologists sort instruments into five classes by what makes the sound, the Hornbostel–Sachs classes: strings, air, solid bodies, stretched skins and electric circuits. Here is one of each, playing Grieg.



  
  
    ▶ Play (1 min)
    ▶ With the mathematics (2½ min)
    Stop
    Full screen
    Ready
  
  Tap an instrument to mute it:
  Grieg's In the Hall of the Mountain King (1875) on a sine theremin (electrophone), a piano (chordophone), a clarinet (aerophone), a glockenspiel (idiophone), and two membranophones, a bass drum and a kettledrum (timpani). There are no recordings: every note is built from pure tones. The struck notes fade, at frequencies computed from each instrument's operator (the bass drum's from the ideal drumhead of the drum page), except the kettledrum's, which are measured, because the drum page's simple model gets only halfway to them; the fading times are illustrative. The clarinet holds a steady tone with the tube's odd multiples strong and the even ones faint, and the theremin a single steady pure tone. Each lane shows its current note's frequencies on the pitch ruler of post 1, whose gray lines are whole-number multiples of one frequency. The arrangement is ours, after the transcription at flutetunes.com. On a small screen, use Full screen with the phone turned sideways.


Listen for the three deciders. The theremin’s circuit has a single mode, so it sounds one pure tone. The piano’s partials sit a little sharp of the lines, set by its spectrum. The clarinet holds one repeating cycle, its strong partials picked by the tube’s modes. The glockenspiel’s overtones sit off the lines but, as played here, fade fast, so the fading leaves a clean note. And the two drums share one skin: on the bass drum its modes fall off the lines and it booms; on the kettledrum the air around the head, the strike point and the fading leave one set of modes near the lines, and it plays a note (the drum page).

title: Instruments, case by case
text:
The instruments, one page each
Each page opens with its puzzle and a demo, then answers in one sentence:


  4aWhy does a light touch make a string jump an octave?A light touch at the middle of a string moves none of its frequencies: it damps every mode that moves under the finger, and the modes left ringing, the even ones, which stand still there, are the partials of a note an octave up.▶ String
  4bWhy is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?A tube closed at one end has its modes only at odd multiples of its lowest frequency, which is half that of an open tube of the same length, so a clarinet sounds almost an octave below a flute of the same length and overblows an octave and a fifth higher; blown, its tone is one repeating cycle with strong odd partials and weak even ones.▶ Flute-like▶ Clarinet-like
  4cWhy does a kalimba sound clean?A tine's overtones sit off the whole-number multiples of its fundamental (6.27×, 17.55×), yet a kalimba sounds clean because those overtones die within a fraction of a second (observed, not derived) and the fundamental rings on alone.▶ Kalimba tine
  4dWhere did the harmonica reed's overtones go?Blown, the reed swings in one repeating cycle just below its own lowest frequency and chops the air into identical puffs, so the steady sound has partials only at whole-number multiples, and the reed's off-line overtones are absent from it.▶ Plucked▶ Blown
  4eWhy do piano tuners stretch octaves?A piano wire's stiffness puts each overtone slightly above its whole-number multiple, so tuners stretch octaves to reduce the beating, a slow wobble in loudness, most at the ends of the keyboard.▶ Exactly 2 : 1▶ Stretched
  4fWhy does a drum thud?An ideal drumhead's frequencies (1, 1.59, 2.14, … times the lowest) fit no pitch, so a plain drum thuds; a kettledrum plays a note because the air the head pushes moves one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, the strike point favours them, and the other modes fade fast.▶ Drum


The sounds in this list are simplified: the octave pair exaggerates the string’s stiffness, and the clarinet-like and flute-like tones are plain sums of whole-number multiples. Each page has the full demo.

title: Instruments, case by case
text:
The recipe on every instrument
Each card runs one instrument through the chain the series follows: Newton’s law on a small piece gives the equation of motion (post 2); the operator is its rule, together with how the object is held; its spectrum is the list of frequencies that rule allows (post 3); on the diagram draws them as stems on the pitch ruler, one stem per mode, called the spectrum diagram; and what you hear says which of the three deciders matters. The stems show the spectrum as multiples of the lowest frequency; the button plays a sound made from it.


A violin string
▶ Playplucked a fifth of the way along



DetailsNewton’s law, the operator and its spectrum


Newton’s law on a short piece of string under tension T, where for small slopes the upward part of each end’s pull is tension times slope: u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx}, with c^2 = T/\mu.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, with both ends tied, u(0) = u(L) = 0.
Its spectrum: X = \sin kx with \sin kL = 0, so k = n\pi/L, \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}.




On the diagram: every stem on a line; plucked a fifth of the way along, the 5th is missing.
What you hear: a clear note at f_1. The pluck point sets the brightness; a light touch at the middle damps the modes that move there and leaves the even ones, a note an octave up: the fading decides.

The violin page → · the operator in post 2


A flute and a clarinet
▶ Flute▶ Clarinetthe tubes’ modes; blown, the clarinet’s sound also has faint even multiples



DetailsNewton’s law, the operator and its spectrum


Newton’s law on a thin slab of air, pushed by a pressure difference, \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x, with squeezed air pushing back, p = -K\xi_x, gives p_{tt} = c^2\,p_{xx}, with c^2 = K/\rho, for the pressure p.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, on pressure shapes. Flute, open at both ends: p(0) = p(L) = 0. Clarinet, closed at the reed: p_x(0) = 0, p(L) = 0.
Its spectrum: flute, \sin kL = 0, so f_n = nc/2L; clarinet, \cos kL = 0, so f_n = (2n-1)c/4L.




On the diagram: the flute’s stems on every line; the clarinet’s only at odd multiples of its lowest frequency, 1 : 3 : 5 : \cdots.
What you hear: blown, one repeating cycle, so partials on every line; the clarinet’s note is almost an octave lower for the same length, with strong odd partials picked by the tube’s modes.

The clarinet page → · the operator in post 2


A kalimba tine
▶ Playthe overtones fade almost at once



DetailsNewton’s law, the operator and its spectrum


Newton’s law on a thin slice of steel, where bending stretches one side and squeezes the other, giving a bending moment M = EI\,u_{xx} and a shear force V = -M_x: \rho S\,u_{tt} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}.
The operator: A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, with \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S; clamped at the bridge (u = u_x = 0), free at the tip (u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0).
Its spectrum: \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1, with \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, so f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi with \beta_nL = 1.875, 4.694, 7.855, \dots.




On the diagram: stems at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, off the lines.
What you hear: a brief click, then a clean note: the overtones die within a fraction of a second (observed, not derived), so the fading decides.

The kalimba page → · the operator in post 2


A harmonica reed
▶ Plucked▶ Blownsame reed, two ways of playing



DetailsNewton’s law, the operator and its spectrum


Newton’s law: the kalimba tine’s, for a small brass bar riveted at one end.
The operator: the tine’s, with \kappa^2 = Eh^2/12\rho for thickness h.
Its spectrum: the same ratios, 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, with f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\,\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}}.




On the diagram: plucked, off the lines like the tine; blown, every stem on a line.
What you hear: plucked, this spectrum; blown, the reed chops the airflow into puffs that repeat exactly, and the sound sits at whole-number multiples of the puff rate: the periodic motion decides.

The harmonica page → · the operator in post 2


A piano wire
▶ Playstiffness exaggerated (B = 0.0012)



DetailsNewton’s law, the operator and its spectrum


Newton’s law on a short piece of stiff wire, where tension pulls it straight and the steel resists bending, the two forces adding: u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx} - \kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}, with c^2 = T/\mu, \kappa^2 = EI/\mu.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, with the ends pinned, u = u_{xx} = 0.
Its spectrum: X = \sin kx with \sin kL = 0 and \lambda = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4, so f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, with f_0 = c/2L and B = \pi^2 EI/TL^2.




On the diagram: each stem a little sharp of its line, more so the higher it is.
What you hear: still a clear note, but an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1 beats, so tuners stretch octaves to reduce the beating: the spectrum decides.

The piano page → · the operator in post 2


A drum
▶ Playstruck about a third of the way out



DetailsNewton’s law, the operator and its spectrum


Newton’s law on a small patch of drumhead, where tension T pulls all around the patch’s edge and the divergence theorem turns the total pull into T\,\Delta u per unit area: \sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u, with \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}, the Laplacian.
The operator: A = -c^2\,\Delta, with c^2 = T/\sigma, and the rim held fixed, u = 0.
Its spectrum: for a round drum of radius a, J_m(ka) = 0 (Bessel functions), with \lambda = c^2k^2, so f_{m,n} = c\,j_{m,n}/2\pi a.




On the diagram: stems at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65, 2.92, … times the lowest, scattered between the lines.
What you hear: a sound that doesn’t repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and that fades fast: a thud. A kettledrum gets its note from all three deciders at once.

The drum page → · the operator in post 2

The orchestra’s other two voices have no page here: the theremin’s circuit is the single-number operator 1/LC of post 2, and the glockenspiel’s bar, free at both ends, is worked out in Did instruments shape our scales?.

title: Instruments, case by case
text:
What we found
Played side by side, the instruments split by which of the three deciders answers their puzzle. The spectrum decides the piano’s stretched octaves and the drum’s thud; the fading decides the kalimba’s clean note and the violin’s touched harmonics; on the kettledrum all three work together; and on the bowed string, the clarinet and the blown harmonica a periodic motion, shaped by the resonator’s modes, puts every partial on a line.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Violin · Kalimba → · Glossary
Listen first: hold the blow button on the clarinet, then switch the same tube to a flute and blow again. The register key (on the flute it stands in for a faster, narrower airstream) makes either tube jump to its next mode.
Skip to what we hear if you only want the answer.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The operator, in one line
Let p(x, t) be the air pressure in the tube minus room pressure, at distance x along the tube, from the reed end, at time t. Newton’s law on a thin slab of air, pushed by the pressure difference across it, together with the way air pushes back when it is squeezed, gives the wave equation, the equation a stretched string also obeys (violin page), now for the pressure: p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx}, where c = \sqrt{K/\rho} is the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C, K the air’s bulk modulus (its resistance to being squeezed) and \rho its density. Post 2 derives it step by step; subscripts are partial derivatives.
So the tube’s operator, the rule that turns a pressure shape into minus its rate of change twice over in time, takes minus c^2 times the curvature of the pressure shape; only the ends differ between a flute and a clarinet. At an open end the air meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure: p = 0. (The air just outside moves with the air inside, so an open end acts as if the tube were slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius, an amount called the end correction.) At the clarinet’s reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move back and forth, and air that never moves feels no net push: the pressure has no slope there, p_x = 0.

The tube’s operator. 
p_{tt} = -A\,p, \qquad A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} \approx (343\ \text{m/s})^2,
 acting on pressure shapes along a tube of length L. Flute, open at both ends: p(0) = p(L) = 0. Clarinet, closed at the reed (x = 0) and open at the bell: p_x(0) = 0 and p(L) = 0. In words: the same rule for both tubes, with different ends.




DetailsThe two end conditions, and what the model leaves out

The first end condition, a value held at zero, is a Dirichlet condition; the second, a condition on the slope, is called a Neumann condition. The model assumes a cylindrical tube, narrow compared with the sound’s wavelength, small pressure changes and no friction at the walls. A real clarinet’s bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers below, not the picture.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Its spectrum
A mode is a pressure shape X(x) that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X; it swings at the frequency f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi, and the list of all the eigenvalues \lambda is the spectrum. The ends decide which shapes are allowed: solving -c^2X'' = \lambda X with each pair of end conditions (fold below) gives the two spectra.



PreciselyThe computation, step by step uses derivatives

1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, the mode equation -c^2X'' = \lambda X becomes X'' = -k^2X, solved by the waves 
X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx, \qquad f = \frac{\sqrt\lambda}{2\pi} = \frac{ck}{2\pi} .

2. The flute: room pressure at both ends. X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, and X(L) = 0 needs \sin kL = 0, so kL = n\pi: one half wave, two half waves, and so on. The eigenvalues are \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and the frequencies f_n = n\,c/2L.
3. The clarinet: no pressure slope at the reed, room pressure at the bell. X'(0) = bk = 0 at the reed forces b = 0, leaving X = \cos kx, and X(L) = 0 at the open end needs \cos kL = 0, so kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. The eigenvalues are \lambda_n = \big((2n-1)\pi c/2L\big)^2 and the frequencies f_n = (2n-1)\,c/4L.



The two spectra.
Flute, open at both ends: modes \sin(n\pi x/L), eigenvalues (n\pi c/L)^2, frequencies f_n = n\,c/2L, that is 1, 2, 3, 4, … times the lowest.
Clarinet, closed at the reed and open at the bell: modes \cos\big((2n-1)\pi x/2L\big), eigenvalues \big((2n-1)\pi c/2L\big)^2, frequencies f_n = (2n-1)\,c/4L, that is 1, 3, 5, 7, … times the lowest.
The lowest frequencies are c/2L and c/4L: a ratio of exactly 2 for the same ideal tube.

On the spectrum diagram, the pitch ruler of post 1 with one stem per mode, the two tubes look like this. The stems mark where modes can sit; their heights carry no meaning here.


  
  
  The tubes' modes, as multiples of each tube's lowest frequency: open at both ends (top), every line; closed at one end (bottom), the odd lines only.


Every free motion of the air is a sum of these modes; post 3 shows why.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Blown: a sustained tube
A blown tube does not ring and fade like a plucked string: the reed or the air jet keeps feeding it, and the air settles into one motion that repeats.
Playing frequency. The clarinet’s reed is a valve: when the pressure in the mouthpiece drops it closes, and when the pressure rises it opens, so the air column drives the reed that feeds it. In normal playing this settles into a periodic oscillation, a self-sustained one (post 3), at a playing frequency close to the tube’s sounding mode from the box above. For the lowest notes that is f_1 = c/4L on the clarinet and c/2L on the flute, with L the tube up to the first open hole: the fingers choose the note by choosing L. On a flute an air jet, blown across the hole at the player’s lips, does the reed’s job.
Waveform: the tube’s modes pick the strong partials. A sound that repeats has partials only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate (post 1), but it may have all of them. So the tube’s modes are odd multiples only, while the clarinet’s sound has even multiples too: weak in the low register, the notes played without the register key, where no mode of the tube supports them, but not absent. Wolfe reports exactly this: in the low register the clarinet’s sound has strong first and third harmonics and weak second and fourth, and from about E4 up the even harmonics become more important. The stems below, like those under the demo at the top, show the blown sounds on a ruler whose gray lines are whole-number multiples of the note being played; the heights are how strong each partial is. The demo’s sound is made this way, a repeating wave with strong odd and faint even multiples, whose exact strengths are an illustrative choice.


  
  
  The blown sounds, as multiples of the note being played: the flute (top) has every whole-number multiple; the clarinet (bottom) has strong odd multiples and faint even ones.


The player’s control. The breath sets how loud and how bright the note is. Blowing harder drives the reed further from gentle, nearly linear motion, which adds high harmonics, so the tone gets brighter as well as louder; played softly, the sound is mellower, with few high harmonics (Wolfe). The note lasts as long as the player keeps blowing.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
What we hear
Almost an octave deeper. The flute’s lowest mode, \sin(\pi x/L), has room pressure at both ends and swings most in the middle: half a wavelength fits in the tube. The clarinet’s, \cos(\pi x/2L), swings most at the reed and has room pressure at the open end: only a quarter of a wavelength fits. A wave twice as long has half the frequency, so the same ideal tube sounds exactly an octave lower closed at one end. Real flutes and clarinets differ a little in length, the clarinet’s mouthpiece and bell change its effective length, and the open ends act slightly longer than they are, so the real interval comes out a bit less than an octave.
Overblowing: an octave or a twelfth. The flute’s spectrum has every whole-number multiple of its lowest frequency; the clarinet’s has only the odd ones, with nothing in between. So when a clarinetist presses the register key, the tube jumps to its next mode, 3 times its lowest frequency, an octave and a fifth, called a twelfth (a fifth is the ratio 3/2). (The demo keeps the low-register tone color when the register key is on.) A flutist overblows with a faster, narrower airstream, and the flute’s next mode is 2 times its lowest, an octave. That is why clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart and flute fingerings an octave apart.



DetailsHow the register key picks out the 3× mode

The clarinet’s register key opens a small hole near the top of the tube. An open hole lets air in and out, pulling the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the lower part of the low register (the notes played without the key), the hole sits about a third of the way down the sounding tube, right where that note’s 3f_1 mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode (Wolfe). For the other notes the hole is off that point, well off for the lowest and highest notes you play with the key (Wolfe), and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, and the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental’s lower frequency it moves more easily, so the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the higher frequency of the 3f_1 mode it moves much less, so the hole acts almost as a plug. Either way the tube jumps to the 3f_1 mode.



The four aspects


The clarinet’s four aspects, read off its blown sound.


Aspect
Clarinet (and flute)




Pitch
the playing frequency, close to the tube’s sounding mode: c/4L for the clarinet’s lowest notes (c/2L for the flute’s), with L chosen by the fingers; the register key jumps to 3\times (the flute overblows to 2\times)


Loudness
the breath: blowing harder is louder


Timbre
in the low register, strong odd partials and weak even ones, picked by the tube’s modes; more even ones higher up; brighter when played louder (Wolfe)


Duration
as long as the player blows





For a sustained instrument the four aspects come from different places than for a ringing one: while the note is held there are no fading times to read; the repeating cycle gives the whole-number multiples, the tube’s modes set which are strong, and the player sets the rest.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
What we found
Air in a tube has the operator A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, the same for both instruments up to the ends. Open at both ends, the flute’s modes sit at every whole-number multiple of c/2L; closed at the reed, the clarinet’s sit at the odd multiples of c/4L, so it sounds almost an octave lower and overblows an octave and a fifth up. Blown, both run one repeating cycle with partials on every line, and the clarinet’s tube makes its odd partials strong: the resonator’s spectrum shapes the periodic tone.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:

References. J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction (strong first and third harmonics in the low register, more even harmonics from about E4; louder playing brighter; the register hole a third of the way down) and Pipes and harmonics, UNSW. N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998: chapter 8 (pipes) and chapter 15 (woodwind reed instruments).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Piano · Beyond · Can you hear the shape of a drum? → · Glossary
Listen first: tap the head anywhere, then tap dead center and compare.
Skip to what we hear if you only want the answer.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
The operator, in one line
Let u(x, y, t) be the height of the head above its rest position at the point (x, y) at time t. The head has mass \sigma per unit area, and its tension T is a force per unit length of any cut through it. Newton’s law on a small patch of the head, with the tension pulling all around the patch’s edge, gives 
\sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy},
 where \Delta u, the Laplacian, adds the second derivatives in the two directions across the sheet (post 2 derives it). In words: on a string, tension pulls each point toward the average height of its two neighbors; on a sheet it pulls each point toward the average height of all the points around it, and \Delta u measures how far a point sits below that average.
The rim completes the operator: it is clamped, so u = 0 there.

The drum’s operator. 
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = -c^2\,\Delta, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\sigma},
 acting on shapes of the head that are zero on the rim. In words: tension pulls each point toward the average of its surroundings, and the rim holds still.




DetailsWhat the model leaves out

The model assumes small slopes, a uniform tension that does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, no air, and no damping or radiation, so its modes never fade; a real head loses its energy to the air quickly, and the air matters, as the two drums further down show.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales: A X = \lambda X, with the number \lambda called its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the head keeps it and swings at the frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, the mode condition is -\Delta X = k^2 X inside the drum, with X = 0 on the rim. For a round drum of radius a, it can be solved by splitting it into a problem around the center and a problem outward from it, a separation of variables.
For a round drum of radius a, write the shape as a function of the distance r from the center times a function of the angle \theta (first fold below). Going around the center, the shape must come back to itself after a turn, which allows only \cos m\theta and \sin m\theta with m a whole number: m straight still lines through the center, like spokes. Outward from the center, the shape is a Bessel function J_m(kr), which plays the part the sine plays on a string: it wiggles like a cosine whose swings slowly shrink (second fold, and the figure).



Step-by-step derivationSeparating the mode equation in polar coordinates uses the chain rule

Distance and angle. In the coordinates r and \theta the Laplacian reads 
\Delta X = X_{rr} + \frac1r X_r + \frac{1}{r^2}X_{\theta\theta}.
 This is a standard change of variables, quoted here; it follows from the chain rule (Laplace operator in polar coordinates).
The split. Substituting X = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta) into -\Delta X = k^2X and multiplying by r^2/(R\Theta) gives 
\frac{r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R}{R} = -\frac{\Theta''}{\Theta}.
 The left side depends only on r, the right only on \theta. Change \theta alone: the left side can’t change, so neither can the right. So both equal one constant. The around part and the outward part are solved in the next fold.





PreciselyAround the center a loop, outward Bessel’s equation uses derivatives

2. Around the center: a loop. Going once around the drum must bring \Theta back to itself, so -\Theta'' = m^2\Theta with \Theta repeating every turn: the eigenvalue problem of a loop of string (post 3). So m is a whole number and \Theta = \cos m\theta or \sin m\theta. A mode with m \ge 1 has m straight still lines through the center, like spokes.
3. Outward from the center: Bessel’s equation. What remains for R is 
r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0,
 Bessel’s equation. It depends on r only through kr, so its solutions are functions of kr. Of its two essentially different solutions, one, the Bessel function J_m(kr), is finite at the center; the other becomes infinite there, which would take infinite energy, so it is not a free mode. J_m plays the part the sine played on a string: it wiggles like a cosine or sine whose swings slowly shrink.













J₀ (starts at 1)J₁ (starts at 0)
2.4055.5208.654
r →

The rim picks out the frequencies. The rim condition R(a) = 0 says J_m(ka) = 0: ka must be a zero of J_m. Writing j_{m,n} for the n-th positive zero, k = j_{m,n}/a. The zeros have no closed form and are computed numerically; those of J_0 are 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, …, in the ratios 1 : 2.30 : 3.60.

The round drum’s spectrum. Modes J_m(j_{m,n}\,r/a)\cos m\theta and J_m(j_{m,n}\,r/a)\sin m\theta, for m = 0, 1, 2, \dots and n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with eigenvalues \lambda_{m,n} = c^2 j_{m,n}^2/a^2 and frequencies 
f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a}.
 In order, relative to the lowest: 1, 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, 2.653, 2.917, … Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to two modes, the cosine and the sine, the same pattern turned.




DetailsWhy these are all the modes, why the pairs are exact, and how the zeros are spaced

These are all the modes: expanding any mode in a Fourier series in \theta reduces -\Delta X = k^2X, term by term, to Bessel’s equation for each m.
Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to exactly two modes because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders never share a positive zero; this was conjectured by Bourget and proved by Carl Ludwig Siegel in 1929. This page computes the zeros numerically. For large n they approach j_{m,n} \approx (n + \tfrac m2 - \tfrac14)\pi: evenly spaced for one fixed m, but shifted by an amount that depends on m. The round head’s symmetry shows up as a multiplicity of 2.


On the spectrum diagram, the pitch ruler of post 1 with one stem per mode, each stem is one j_{m,n}/j_{0,1} from your last strike. After 1×, the next few sit between the lines. Higher up the stems crowd together, so some land near a line by chance, such as 2.92× and 4.06×; but no base frequency in the range we hear as pitch puts them all on or near lines. Each stem’s height is how strongly that mode sounds at the listening ring for the strike you made: strike somewhere else and the heights change, never the positions. Tap a stem to see that mode on the drumhead and hear it alone.


    Partials of the last strike · tap a stem

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Struck: a ringing drumhead
A struck head rings: it moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum a_{m,n} X_{m,n}\,e^{-t/\tau_{m,n}} \cos(2\pi f_{m,n} t + \phi_{m,n}), each with its own fading time \tau_{m,n}, so its sound is a sum of partials at the frequencies of the spectrum. The demo at the top is made this way, with illustrative fading times.
Frequencies: between the lines. They are the zeros of the Bessel functions, scaled: 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, 2.65×, 2.92×, …, scattered between the lines (fold below).



DetailsWhy the zeros miss the lines

The frequencies are the zeros of the Bessel functions, scaled. For the modes with no spokes, the zeros of J_0 come at nearly even steps, about \pi apart, but the first one is short, about 0.77\pi rather than \pi, so the later zeros are not multiples of the first: the frequencies go 1 : 2.30 : 3.60. Each number of spokes gives its own sequence, shifted by a different amount, and the sequences interleave at unrelated places. Merged, they give the drum’s list 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, 2.65×, 2.92×, …, scattered between the lines.


Amounts: where you strike. A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. Every mode with spokes stays still at the center, so a strike at dead center sounds only the round modes, those with no spokes; a strike on one of a mode’s still lines leaves that mode silent.



DetailsHow strongly a strike excites each mode, in this model uses integrals over an area

Number the modes X_1, X_2, \dots in order of frequency. A sharp strike, a brief push at a point p, gives mode i a starting speed in proportion to X_i(p), the mode’s height at the point struck, the same rule as the piano’s hammer. We model what you hear as the speed of the head at a listening point q, which picks up mode i in proportion to X_i(q). Dividing by \iint X_i^2\,dA, the integral of the mode’s square over the head, removes the arbitrary size of each shape. So mode i sounds with weight X_i(p)\,X_i(q)\big/\iint X_i^2\,dA. (A real drum radiates sound from its whole head, and some modes radiate better than others; this model ignores that.)


A mode’s still lines can be seen with sand. Sprinkle it on a vibrating sheet, and it is jostled wherever the sheet moves and comes to rest where it doesn’t, so each pattern is one mode’s still lines, the places where a strike would leave that mode silent. Ernst Chladni showed this on metal plates in the 1780s; here is the same trick on a drumhead: pick a frequency and watch where the sand goes.


  
  
  Sprinkle fresh sandHear this note
  
  Each button drives the drumhead at one of its own frequencies, given as a multiple of the lowest. Every grain is jostled in proportion to how much the head moves under it, so grains drift until they reach a place where the head stays still. Chladni used stiff metal plates, whose operator involves bending, not tension; the sand behaves the same way on both.





PreciselyWhere the sand collects, and the history uses polar coordinates

The mode J_m(kr)\cos m\theta with k = j_{m,n}/a is zero where \cos m\theta = 0, at 2m angles, which pair up into m lines through the center, and along the circles where J_m(kr) = 0 inside the rim, n - 1 of them for the n-th zero. Those are exactly the lines where the sand collects.
In 1808 Chladni showed the French Institute in Paris, the body that then held the Academy of Sciences, his sand patterns on plates bowed along their edges. Napoleon offered a prize for explaining them. Sophie Germain won it in 1816, the first woman to receive the Paris Academy’s grand prize in mathematics, with a theory that was still incomplete; Gustav Kirchhoff gave the full theory of vibrating plates, with the correct edge conditions, in 1850. Finding the still lines and finding the frequencies are one problem: on a drumhead, the one on this page; on a plate, the same problem with the plate’s own operator.


Fading, and muffling. A real head gives its energy to the air quickly, so the sound fades fast; the round modes, which pump air like a piston, go first. How long a bass drum rings is also the player’s choice: players muffle the head with a leg or a towel when the music calls for short notes, and let it ring for long ones (Aleo, Interlochen 2023).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
One drumhead, two drums
A bass drum and a kettledrum (one of the timpani) share this operator, yet one booms and the other plays a note. Step through the three things that separate them: where the head is struck, what surrounds it, and which modes fade first. On the kettledrum, the air the head must push pulls the spoke modes, those with one or more lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim, close to 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a common base (HyperPhysics; Fletcher and Rossing), and the strike point and the fast fading of the round modes leave mostly those.



  
    1 · Same head
    2 · Where you strike
    3 · The air adds mass
    4 · What surrounds each head
    5 · What fades
  
  
  
  Each picture is one mode seen from above, labelled (m, n): m still lines through the center, n still circles counting the rim. Dark and light patches move in opposite directions. The ring gives its kind:
  
    round modes: no line through the center (m = 0)
    spoke modes: lines through the center, no circle inside the rim (n = 1)

    Air's added mass, 2ρa/σ
    Kettle stiffness (raises the lowest round mode's λ by this fraction)
  
  Each stem is one mode: its position is its frequency as a multiple of a base an octave below the (1,1) mode, so the (1,1) sits at 2×, and its height is how strongly the strike starts it; dashed stems are modes that have faded. Stems on the dashed whole-number lines make a note. Each drum plays at its own size: the bass drum's lowest mode near 50 Hz, the timpani's (1,1) at 131 Hz (C3). Measured ratios puts the kettledrum's spoke modes on 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 times the base, the pattern a kettledrum measured by Benade sits close to (about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times its lowest mode, as tabulated by HyperPhysics), which this toy model gets only halfway to. A toy model; the fold below gives its numbers and what it misses.





DetailsThe toy model, the kettle, and other drums uses integrals over an area

Where each drum is struck. A concert bass drum is played slightly off center; center playing, punchier and with less sustain, is kept for rhythmic passages (Graham 2017; Aleo, Interlochen 2023). There the spoke modes move little, so among the lowest modes the round ones dominate. Players muffle the head with a leg or a towel when the music calls for short notes, and let it ring for long ones (Aleo, Interlochen 2023); the step-through’s Muffle button does the first. Timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out (HyperPhysics), roughly a third of the way in from the rim (Graham 2017). With the weight |X(p)|\big/\big(\iint X^2\,dA\big)^{1/2} for a strike at p, on a head of radius 1, the lowest round mode (0,1) has 1.09 at the center, 0.73 at halfway and 0.37 at three-quarters, while the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) have between 0.74 and 1.19 anywhere from halfway to three-quarters: lower than the spoke modes’ across the whole range. Nearer halfway the stick also sits close to the inner still circles of the modes (0,2), (1,2), (2,2) and (3,2), which lie between 0.44 and 0.65 of the radius, which quiets those too. The clear note also relies on the remaining modes being weaker or fading faster, which this page takes from measurements (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 18) rather than deriving.
The air’s mass. Treat the air on both sides of the head as not squeezable, and each mode, locally, as a ripple of wavenumber k = j_{m,n}/a, whose crests are about \pi/k apart. The air such a ripple sets moving reaches about 1/k from the head on each side, which adds a mass of about 2\rho/k per unit area (\rho \approx 1.2 kg/m³ for air) to the head’s own \sigma: 
\omega^2 = \frac{T k^2}{\sigma + 2\rho/k}, \qquad f \propto \frac{k}{\sqrt{\sigma + 2\rho/k}} ,
 so coarse shapes, with small k, slow down most. This is added mass: it can only lower frequencies. A typical Mylar kettledrum head has \sigma \approx 0.26 kg/m², on the two drums Packer studied, radii 0.32 and 0.355 m (Packer 1993, appendix B); with a = 0.33 m, 2\rho a/\sigma \approx 3.0. The spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) move from 1 : 1.34 : 1.67 : 1.98 to 1 : 1.42 : 1.83 : 2.24, halfway to 1.5 : 2 : 2.5. The rest of the shift comes from a full calculation of the air inside and around a finite head (Christian, Davis, Tubis, Anderson, Mills and Rossing 1984), not from the kettle’s air spring, its uniform pressure.
The kettle. The nearly sealed kettle (it has a small vent) acts as a spring on the volume the head sweeps, V = \iint u\,dA, adding \tfrac12\eta V^2 to the stored energy for some constant \eta > 0. The operator gains the term (\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle, where \mathbf 1 is the constant shape and \sigma the head’s mass per unit area: a term of rank one. Every mode with m \ge 1 has \iint X\,dA = 0, because \int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0, so \big(A + (\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle\big)X = AX, and in this model it keeps its frequency exactly. Only the round modes are raised, and since the new term couples them to each other, their shapes change too; the explorable treats each on its own. In general, added stiffness never lowers a frequency and added mass never raises one, by the min–max principle.
The bass drum’s second head. A bass drum has a head on each end of its shell, coupled through the air inside, which splits its two lowest modes, (0,1) and (1,1); the two heads’ lowest modes are commonly tuned about a fourth apart (HyperPhysics). Not modelled here.
Other drums. Toms are tuned to rough pitches, and a snare drum’s crack comes from the wires, the snares, stretched across its lower head. The tabla and the mridangam reach near-whole-number overtones a different way: a patch of paste loads the center of the head, which makes the head’s density non-uniform, outside this page’s model (Raman and Kumar 1920; Raman 1934).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
What we hear
Off the lines and fading fast: a thud. An ideal head’s frequencies don’t sit at whole-number multiples of any base frequency we hear as pitch, so its sound doesn’t repeat at any such rate; and a real head gives its energy to the air quickly, so it fades fast. Together, a thud: the spectrum decides; where you strike changes only how loud each mode is.
A kettledrum’s note. On a kettledrum all three deciders point the same way. The air the head drags along moves the spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base (the spectrum); the stick, between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, starts the lowest round mode more weakly than the spoke modes (the playing); and the round modes radiate their energy away within a fraction of a second (the fading). What is left nearly repeats: a note. Players and acousticians name it at the lowest of those modes, the (1,1) mode, the drum’s “principal tone” (Vienna’s Institute of Musical Acoustics).



PreciselyWhich octave the ear names

The modes above the (1,1) sit a fifth, an octave and a major tenth (ratio 5 : 2) above it. The pitch rule of post 1 would put the pitch an octave lower, at the base, and HyperPhysics notes that the missing-fundamental effect might give the drum that lower pitch; which octave the ear names is one of the exceptions post 1 lists, and this series doesn’t settle it.



The four aspects


The two drums’ four aspects.


Aspect
Bass drum
Kettledrum




Pitch
no clear pitch: the modes sit off the lines
a note, named at the (1,1) mode; the head’s tension tunes it


Loudness
how hard the head is struck
how hard the head is struck


Timbre
mostly round modes, from a strike near the center: a boom
spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, left by the strike point and the fading


Duration
fast fading, or shorter still when muffled
the spoke modes ring on after the round ones die

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
What we found
An ideal drumhead, A = -c^2\Delta with the rim held still, has its frequencies at the zeros of Bessel functions, off the lines, so a plain drum thuds: the spectrum decides. A kettledrum is the same head in different surroundings, where the spectrum, the playing and the fading work together: the air pulls its spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, and the strike point and the fast-fading round modes leave mostly those, a note.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
Next
