title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Harmonica · Bass drum and kettledrum → · Glossary
Listen first: an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1, then a stretched one. The slow wobble in loudness is called a beat.
Skip to what we hear if you only want the answer.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
The operator, in one line
Let u(x, t) be the height of a piano wire above its rest line. Two forces act on each short piece of it, and they add: tension pulls it like a violin string, and stiff steel pushes back against bending like a kalimba tine. Newton’s law on a short piece (post 2 derives it) gives 
u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx} - \kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\mu},
 with T the tension, \mu the mass per unit length, E steel’s Young’s modulus and I = \pi d^4/64 the second moment of area of a round wire of diameter d; subscripts are partial derivatives. The ends complete the operator. The bridge at one end and a metal bearing point at the other hold the wire in place, so u = 0 there; if they let it pivot freely they exert no bending moment, which reads u_{xx} = 0. These are called pinned ends; real piano strings are held a little more firmly, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.

The piano wire’s operator. The equation of motion is u_{tt} = -A\,u, with 
A = -c^2\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \kappa^2\frac{d^4}{dx^4},
 acting on shapes with u = u_{xx} = 0 at both ends. The first term is the string’s operator, from tension; the second is the kalimba’s, from bending: operators add. In words: the force per unit mass on each point is the string’s pull toward the inside of the curve plus the bar’s push back against bending.




DetailsWhat the model leaves out

The model assumes a plain steel wire (bass strings are wound with copper, which adds mass but little stiffness), small slopes, a uniform wire and no damping; the fading is added back below.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales: A X = \lambda X, with the number \lambda called its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the wire keeps it and swings at the frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Each sine \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfies the pinned ends, and both terms of A only rescale it, by c^2k^2 and \kappa^2k^4 with k = n\pi/L; so the sines are the modes and the two eigenvalues add (fold below).



PreciselyThe computation, step by step uses derivatives and square roots

1. Try a sine, which already satisfies the pinned ends. Take X = \sin(kx) with k = n\pi/L, where L is the wire’s length and n = 1, 2, 3, \dots It is zero at both ends, and so is X'' = -k^2X: both pinned conditions hold.
2. Apply the operator: each term rescales the same sine. Two derivatives give X'' = -k^2X and four give X'''' = k^4X, so 
A X = \big(c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4\big)\,X .
 The sine is rescaled, not reshaped: it is an eigenfunction, with eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4. The string’s eigenvalue and the bar’s simply add, because with pinned ends the two operators share their eigenfunctions. There are no other modes: the sines already form a complete set (post 3), and since the operator is symmetric, an eigenfunction for any other eigenvalue would be perpendicular to every sine, hence zero.
3. The frequencies: the string’s, nudged up by stiffness. Factoring out the string’s part, \lambda_n = c^2k^2\big(1 + (EI/T)\,k^2\big), and with k = n\pi/L, taking the square root and dividing by 2\pi gives the result.



The piano wire’s spectrum. Modes \sin(n\pi x/L), n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with frequencies 
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{T L^2}.
 Here f_0 = c/2L is the lowest frequency the same wire would have without stiffness; the actual fundamental is f_1 = f_0\sqrt{1 + B}. Each partial sits at f_n/f_1 = n\sqrt{(1 + Bn^2)/(1 + B)} times the fundamental: a little above n, more so the larger n.

The stiffness constant B is small, but it multiplies n^2, so the fundamental barely moves while high partials run noticeably sharp: the string is slightly inharmonic.
For a middle C wire B is roughly 4.4\times10^{-4}, which puts the 10th partial about 37 cents, a third of a semitone, sharp of ten times the fundamental (fold below). Since I grows like the fourth power of the diameter and B falls like 1/L^2, short treble strings, thick for their length, are the stiffest.



DetailsHow big is B? A middle C wire uses logarithms

For a middle C wire, roughly d = 1 mm and L = 0.6 m, with steel’s E = 2\times10^{11} Pa and density 7850 kg/m³; a tension of about 610 N then gives middle C. So I \approx 4.9\times10^{-14} m^4 and B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}. The 10th partial (the fundamental counts as the 1st), at 10f_0\sqrt{1 + 100B}, then sits 1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental, about a third of a semitone. These numbers are rough; real strings vary.


On the spectrum diagram, the pitch ruler of post 1 with one stem per mode, here are the frequencies of a piano note, middle C, or the last key you played on the keyboard further down. Each stem is one f_n/f_1 from the box above, with that key’s B. They sit a little sharp of the gray lines, the more so the higher the partial; the readout gives the shift in cents, hundredths of a semitone. Each stem’s height is how strongly the hammer starts that mode, as the next section explains.


    Partials of the last key
    
    
    Try the soft pedal or the practice mute on the keyboard below: the high stems shrink, but none of them moves.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
Struck: a ringing string
A struck wire rings: it moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum_n a_n\,e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), and the sound passed on by the soundboard keeps those frequencies and fading times (post 3). The demos are made this way.
Frequencies: just sharp of the lines, as the spectrum says; the low partials sit close enough for one clear note.
Amounts: the hammer. A hammer blow starts each mode in proportion to the mode’s own height where the hammer hits, so a mode that stands still there stays silent. In the demos the hammer strikes an eighth of the way along, where the 8th and 16th modes stand still, so those two are nearly silent. How hard the key is struck matters too, and not only for loudness: the hammer’s felt acts as a spring that gets stiffer the harder it is squashed, so a heavy blow acts like a hard spring and starts many more high partials, and loud notes sound brighter than soft ones (Russell; post 1 and post 2).



DetailsFading in two stages: the coupled strings

Fading: two stages. Each mode fades at its own rate, the high ones faster in the demos, whose fading times are illustrative. Most notes have two or three strings, and Weinreich showed that their coupling through the bridge, each string’s motion slightly shaking the others, produces the piano’s two-stage decay: a loud start that fades fast, then a quiet, long aftersound. Post 3 places that coupled pair among the equations with friction; the demos leave the coupling out.


The player’s damping: dampers and pedals. Letting go of a key drops a felt damper on its strings, which drains each mode in proportion to how much it moves under the felt; the pedals act on the dampers or on the blow. Every control a pianist touches changes how strongly the modes start or how fast they die; only the tuner’s wrench, which changes the tension, moves the frequencies.



DetailsWhat each control changes




Control
What it changes
Effect




key held down
lifts that note’s damper
the note rings


key released
drops the damper on the string
the modes die, each at its own rate


sustain pedal (right)
lifts every damper
released notes ring on


soft pedal (left)
the hammer blow: on a grand it strikes fewer strings, with a softer part of its felt; on an upright it starts closer to the strings
quieter; high modes weaker


practice mute (middle, on uprights)
the hammer blow: a felt strip sits between hammer and string
much quieter; most high modes gone


tuning pin
the operator: the tension
every frequency moves



On a grand piano the middle pedal is usually the sostenuto, which holds up only the dampers of keys already down.





Step-by-step derivationThe full string equation, the hammer weights and the damping rates uses integrals of products of modes and a first-order approximation

The operator is only part of the string’s equation. A real string is also pushed by the hammer and loses energy to damping; here f(x,t) is a force, not a frequency: 
\mu\,u_{tt} + b(x,t)\,u_t = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} + f(x,t).
 Each term has one job. The operator’s term, T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} (that is, -\mu A u), fixes the frequencies and the mode shapes. The forcing f is the hammer, and it fixes how much of each mode is excited. The damping b is the felt dampers plus small internal losses, and it fixes how fast each mode dies. In the table above, the dampers and the sustain pedal change b; the soft pedal and the practice mute change f; only the tuning pin changes the operator.
1. Expand in modes. Write u(x,t) = \sum_n q_n(t)\,X_n(x), with X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L), A X_n = \omega_n^2X_n and the pinned conditions.
2. Project. Substitute into the full equation, multiply by X_m and integrate along the string. The operator is symmetric with these boundary conditions (in fact self-adjoint), by integrating by parts, so the X_n are orthogonal: \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n. The acceleration and operator terms collapse to one term each: 
\mu N_m\,(\ddot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m) + \sum_n D_{mn}\,\dot q_n = F_m(t),
 with N_m = \int X_m^2\,dx, D_{mn} = \int b\,X_mX_n\,dx and F_m = \int f\,X_m\,dx.
3. The hammer. The felt touches a short stretch near x_h, so F_m(t) \approx X_m(x_h)\,P(t), where P(t) is the total force. Every mode gets the same push in time, weighted by X_m(x_h): the mode’s own height at the hammer.
4. The damper. If the damping is weak, the cross terms D_{mn} with m \ne n change the answer only at second order. Keeping the diagonal leaves a damped oscillator for each mode, 
\ddot q_m + 2\gamma_m\,\dot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m = 0, \qquad \gamma_m = \frac{D_{mm}}{2\mu N_m},
 whose solution e^{-\gamma_m t}\cos\big(\sqrt{\omega_m^2 - \gamma_m^2}\,t\big) decays at the rate \gamma_m while its frequency moves only by order \gamma_m^2/\omega_m. For a felt on a short stretch W of the string, \gamma_m = \int_W b\,X_m^2\,dx \big/ 2\mu\int_0^L X_m^2\,dx: a mode is damped in proportion to how much it moves under the felt, and a mode with a node under the felt barely notices the damper.
5. Honest limits. A real damper is not weak: it stops a note in a fraction of a second. The formula gives the right picture, that modes are damped by how much they move under the felt, but not exact decay times.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
What we hear
Why exact octaves beat. A tuner sets an octave by ear, listening for beats between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Two nearly equal frequencies played together beat at a rate equal to their difference. The spectrum says where the lower note’s second partial sits: 
\frac{f_2}{f_1} = 2\sqrt{\frac{1 + 4B}{1 + B}} \approx 2\Big(1 + \frac{3B}{2}\Big),
 using \sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 + x/2 and 1/\sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 - x/2 for small x. So the second partial is more than twice the fundamental, by a factor of about 1 + 3B/2. An upper note tuned to exactly twice the fundamental sits just below it, and the two beat. Raising the upper note slows this beat and makes the octave slightly wider than 2 : 1. Tuners also listen to other pairs, such as the lower note’s fourth partial against the upper note’s second, and the upper note’s own partials run sharp too, so stiffness makes it impossible to silence all of the beats at once: real tuning is a compromise. Tick “Play every partial” in the demo at the top to hear it: the stretched octave then wobbles too. On a stiff string, “exactly 2 : 1” lines up the wrong pair of frequencies.
The stretch is largest at the ends of the keyboard. Repeated octave by octave across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: compared with equal temperament, the top of a piano ends up sharp and the bottom flat. Two things make the stretch grow toward the ends. The small widenings add up, octave by octave, away from the middle; and the most inharmonic strings are at the two ends: the short treble strings, and the bass strings, which the size of the piano keeps short for their pitch. O. L. Railsback measured this stretch on pianos tuned by ear in the 1930s; the plot of how far each note sits from equal temperament is called the Railsback curve: close to equal temperament in the middle of the keyboard, flat in the bass, sharp in the treble.

The four aspects


The piano’s four aspects.


Aspect
Piano




Pitch
the fundamental f_1 = f_0\sqrt{1 + B}, set by the tuner through the tension; the low partials sit close enough to the lines for one clear note


Loudness
how hard the key is struck


Timbre
the partials’ slight sharpness; the hammer’s strike point; a harder blow brighter; the two-stage decay; the soft pedal and practice mute, which soften the blow


Duration
how long the key is held, or the sustain pedal; the strings’ own fading, two-stage; the top keys have no dampers and die by themselves

Reader questionWhat does a damper do, and what would a piano without dampers sound like?

Without dampers, releasing a key would do nothing: every string would ring until it died on its own, exactly as if the sustain pedal were always down. On a real piano each key lifts a felt damper off its strings; letting go drops the damper back and stops the note within a fraction of a second. The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers at once, so released notes keep ringing. The keyboard above models both. The top 20 keys have no dampers at all, as on a real piano: those short strings die out quickly by themselves.


For the inside of a piano, hammers, dampers and pedals, see the standalone post A Piano: the whole upright, all 88 keys, with its pedals.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
What we found
A piano wire is a string and a bar at once, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, and its spectrum, f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, puts each partial slightly above its whole-number multiple. So an exact 2 : 1 octave beats, and tuners stretch octaves, most at the ends of the keyboard: the spectrum decides. The hammer, the dampers and the pedals change how the modes start and die, not where they sit.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Clarinet · Harmonica → · Glossary
Listen first: tap a tine. Then tick the box that keeps the overtones ringing, and tap it again.
Skip to what we hear if you only want the answer.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
The operator, in one line
A string springs back because it is stretched; a tine is under no tension at all, and springs back because steel resists being bent. Let u(x, t) be the tine’s height at distance x from the clamp at time t. Newton’s law on a thin slice of the tine, with the forces that bending sets up inside it, gives the beam equation u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}, with four derivatives along the tine where a string had two; post 2 derives it, as the Euler–Bernoulli beam. The constant is \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S: E is steel’s Young’s modulus, how stiff the material is; I the second moment of area of the cross-section, how strongly its shape resists bending; \rho the density and S the cross-section’s area.
The ends complete the operator. At the base the tine is held down, so it can neither move nor tilt: u = 0 and u_x = 0. A bar held this way at one end and free at the other is called a cantilever. At the free tip nothing bends or pushes the bar: the bending moment, the turning effect that bends it, and the shear force, the sideways force across a cut, both vanish, which reads u_{xx} = 0 and u_{xxx} = 0.

The tine’s operator. 
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = \kappa^2\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S},
 with u = u_x = 0 at the clamp and u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 at the tip. In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point back is the fourth derivative of the shape, times a constant set by the steel and the cross-section. The string’s operator was -c^2\,d^2/dx^2: two derivatives instead of four.

What four derivatives do. Squeeze a shape into half the length, and every rate of change along it doubles. A string’s pull depends on its curvature, a rate of change of a rate of change: 2 × 2 = 4 times harder. A tine’s push depends on how that curvature itself changes along the tine, twice over: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 times harder. Both of the tine’s surprises below come from this. The model assumes small slopes, a uniform bar clamped at exactly one point, and no damping or sound radiation: in the model every mode rings forever, and how fast each one dies is taken from measurement.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X(x) that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X. Such a shape swings at the frequency f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi, and the list of all the eigenvalues \lambda is the operator’s spectrum. For the tine, the mode equation is \kappa^2 X'''' = \lambda X.
1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? Write \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, so that X'''' = \beta^4 X: four derivatives give back the shape, times \beta^4. Four functions do this: \cos\beta x and \sin\beta x, whose sign flips cancel after four derivatives, and \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2 are the hyperbolic functions, whose derivatives are each other, (\cosh y)' = \sinh y and (\sinh y)' = \cosh y, with no sign changes at all. So X is a combination of the four, with four unknown constants.
2. The ends pick the shapes. The four end conditions are four equations for those four constants. They have a solution other than all zero exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 ,
 the mode condition, worked out in the fold below.
3. Find the roots. Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be close to 0, so \beta L sits near (n - \tfrac12)\pi, closer and closer as n grows. Solved numerically, the roots are \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots; the first is the furthest from its estimate, \pi/2 \approx 1.571.



DetailsThe mode condition from the four end conditions uses a 2×2 determinant

The clamped end. X(0) = 0 and X'(0) = 0 leave two constants: 
X = a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x) .

The free tip. Differentiating, and dropping the common factors \beta^2 and \beta^3, the conditions X''(L) = 0 and X'''(L) = 0 read, with the shorthand c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L, s_2 = \sinh\beta L: 
\begin{gathered}
-(c_1 + c_2)\,a - (s_1 + s_2)\,b = 0, \\
(s_1 - s_2)\,a - (c_1 + c_2)\,b = 0 .
\end{gathered}

When is there a mode? Two equations pa + qb = 0 and ra + sb = 0 have a solution other than a = b = 0 exactly when ps - qr = 0, the determinant (solve the first for a and substitute into the second). Here 
(c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) = c_1^2 + s_1^2 + 2c_1c_2 + c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 2 + 2c_1c_2 = 0,
 using c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1 and c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1 (multiply out the definitions). So the tine has a mode exactly when \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1. The modes are X_n = \cosh\beta_n x - \cos\beta_n x - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_n x - \sin\beta_n x), with \sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL) from the second equation.



The tine’s spectrum. Eigenvalues \lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4, with \beta_nL = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548, \dots the roots of \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1, and frequencies 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\,(\beta_nL)^2}{2\pi L^2} .
 Since f_n \propto (\beta_nL)^2, the frequency ratios are 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39 : \cdots, growing like (2n-1)^2: off the whole numbers.




DetailsCompare pinned ends: why the clamp and the free tip matter

Compare pinned ends. A bar held in place at both ends but free to pivot has u = u_{xx} = 0 at each end. Then the shapes \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfy all four conditions, four derivatives multiply them by (n\pi/L)^4, and the ratios are 1 : 4 : 9 : 16: whole numbers. If every root of the clamped–free tine sat exactly at (n - \tfrac12)\pi, its ratios would be the whole numbers 1 : 9 : 25 too; the shift of the first root, set by the clamp and the free tip, is what puts them off the lines.


On the spectrum diagram, the pitch ruler of post 1 with one stem per mode, one tine’s frequencies are 1×, then 6.27×, off the gray whole-number lines, and further up 17.55× and 34.39×, off the right edge. Each stem’s height is how hard that mode pushes sideways on the bridge just after a pluck (next section). Tap a stem to see the shape of that mode.


    Modes of one tine · tap a stem

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
Plucked: a ringing tine
A plucked tine rings: it moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum_n a_n\,e^{-t/\tau_n}X_n(x)\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), each fading at its own rate, and the sound reaching you keeps those frequencies and fading times, with amounts changed by the bridge and the body (post 3).
Frequencies: off the lines. They are the spectrum above: 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times the fundamental. Higher modes bend in shorter humps, and for a tine shorter humps push back much harder, so the frequencies grow like the square of the mode number instead of the number itself.
Amounts: the click. You might guess the overtone is too quiet to hear. It isn’t. In how far the tine swings, the overtone is tiny, 2.5% of the fundamental; but the body hears the push on the bridge, not the swing, and in that push the overtone starts strong, about 55% of the fundamental in the sideways force (fold below). That strong start is the click at the beginning of each note.



Step-by-step derivationHow strongly a pluck at the tip excites each mode uses integration by parts

Chapman measured the tines of one kalimba, a Hugh Tracey pentatonic, and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack. A real tine is clamped a little behind the bridge and rests on the bridge partway along, rather than being perfectly clamped at one point, and he found that the measured ratios depend on how the bridge divides the tine’s length, which is one reason they spread. The steps below compute, for the ideal tine, how much of each mode a pluck starts. In short: in displacement, the second mode starts at only 2.5% of the first; but at the clamp, where in this ideal model the tine presses on the bridge, it starts at about 16% of the first in bending moment and 55% in shear force. Those are two different measures of the push on the bridge, not a range of uncertainty.

The pluck shape. Before release, a push F at the tip holds the tine still in a bent shape u_0, so the bar’s restoring force balances the push.
Split it into modes. Write u_0 = \sum_n a_n X_n, with each mode scaled so that \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L. Inside the tine nothing pushes, so EI\,u_0'''' = 0 there; the push enters only at the tip, as the shear force there. Now compute \int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx in two ways. First, EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n (the mode equation, with \omega_n = 2\pi f_n), and the modes are perpendicular, \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n, so only the a_n term survives: the integral is \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,a_n. Second, integrate by parts four times to move the derivatives onto u_0. Inside, EI\,u_0'''' = 0; at the clamp both u_0 and X_n vanish with their slopes; at the tip X_n'' = X_n''' = 0 and u_0'' = 0. The one term left is the tip’s shear force times X_n(L), which is F\,X_n(L). So \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,a_n = F\,X_n(L): mode n behaves like a spring of stiffness proportional to \omega_n^2, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip, and it gives way by force over stiffness.
Tip values. Use the modes in the form of the fold above, with \sigma_n about 0.734 and 1.018 for the first two modes. Written this way, each mode already has \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L, and its tip value is \pm2 for every n (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2, and a_2/a_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%.
Forces. In this model the tine is clamped right at the bridge, so the forces at the clamp are the forces on the bridge. The bending moment at the clamp is EI\,u_{xx} there, and the shear force EI\,u_{xxx} there (up to sign). From the form above, X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2 and X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3. Multiplying by a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2 \propto 1/\beta_n^4, the second mode’s moment at the clamp is (\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 = (1.875/4.694)^2 \approx 16\% of the first’s, and its shear force (\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%.



Fading: the overtones go first. What keeps the note clean is that the overtone dies within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. That fast decay is observed, not derived: the model has no damping, and this page takes the decay from measurement. The acoustician D. M. F. Chapman found exactly this pattern on a real kalimba: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, which dies away so fast that it is heard only at the instant the note starts. A kalimba has no dampers; a note rings until it fades, unless a finger stops the tine.
The demo’s sound is made exactly this way: it adds up the first five modes at the frequencies of the spectrum, each starting with its shear-force strength from the fold above (55% for the second mode). The fundamental fades over a couple of seconds and the overtones within a small fraction of that; those fading times are an illustrative choice consistent with Chapman’s observation, not computed. Tick the box and every mode fades as slowly as the fundamental.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
What we hear
A click, then a clean note. The off-line overtones start strong, which is the click, and die within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. The fundamental left on its own is a single partial, and a sound with one partial has a clear pitch, at its frequency. If every overtone rang as long as the fundamental, the same spectrum would clang; the fading decides. With the box ticked, the off-line overtones keep ringing, and the same tine clangs like a bell.
Half the length, two octaves up. The spectrum says f_n = \kappa(\beta_nL)^2/(2\pi L^2), and the numbers \beta_nL do not depend on the length: so a tine’s frequency goes as one over its length squared. Half the length gives 4 times the frequency, two octaves, where a string, with f \propto 1/L, rises only an octave. That is why the low tines in the demo are not twice as long as the high ones an octave up. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length (Kalimba Magic), and the 1/L^2 makes a small slide go a long way.

The four aspects


The kalimba’s four aspects.


Aspect
Kalimba




Pitch
the fundamental, f_1 \propto 1/L^2, set by the tine’s free length beyond the bridge


Loudness
how far the tine is pushed before it is let go, since every amount grows with it


Timbre
the click: off-line overtones that start strong and die at once; then the fundamental alone


Duration
how long the fundamental takes to fade, or until a finger stops the tine

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
What we found
A tine is a bar clamped at one end, A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, and its spectrum puts the overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, off the whole-number multiples. The pluck starts the first overtone strongly, the click; the fading, observed on real kalimbas rather than derived, removes it within a fraction of a second and leaves the fundamental alone: a clean note.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
Next
A harmonica reed is the same kind of bar, with the same off-line overtones; blown, though, its notes land exactly on the lines: where did the overtones go?

References. D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, paper 5aMUf1, Acoustical Society of America, 2008. Wikipedia, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and Cantilever, and Inharmonicity for a bell’s spectrum. Kalimba Magic, on tuning tines. N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 2 (bars).

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Kalimba · Piano → · Glossary
Listen first: pluck the reed, then blow it, and compare the stems with the gray whole-number lines.
Skip to what we hear if you only want the answer.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
The operator, in one line
A reed is a thin brass bar, riveted at one end over a slot and free at the other: the same kind of bar as a kalimba tine, so it has the same equation, derived in post 2. With u(x, t) the reed’s sideways displacement at distance x from the rivet, the beam equation u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx}, in which the brass’s resistance to bending pulls each point back by the fourth derivative of the shape, reads u_{tt} = -Au, and the ends complete the operator: at the rivet the reed can neither move nor tilt, u = u_x = 0; at the free tip nothing bends or pushes it, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0.

The reed’s operator is the tine’s: 
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = \kappa^2\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S} = \frac{E h^2}{12\rho},
 with u = u_x = 0 at the rivet and u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 at the tip. Here E is brass’s Young’s modulus, \rho its density, S the area of the reed’s cross-section and I its second moment of area; the last form of \kappa^2 is for a rectangular reed of width w and thickness h, where I = wh^3/12 and S = wh. In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point back is the fourth derivative of the shape, times a constant set by the brass and the thickness.




DetailsWhat the model leaves out

The model assumes small motions, a uniform bar clamped at exactly one point, no damping and no air around the reed. Real reeds are not exactly uniform, so their overtones differ somewhat from the ideal values below.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
Its spectrum
A mode is a shape the operator only rescales, AX = \lambda X; its frequency is f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi, and the list of eigenvalues is the spectrum. The operator and the end conditions are the tine’s, so the spectrum is too: the kalimba page writes \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4 and finds a mode exactly when \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1, with roots \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548, \dots

The reed’s spectrum. Eigenvalues \lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4, frequencies f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi, in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : \cdots, off the whole-number lines, with the lowest 
f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}} .
 The width w cancels: it decides how much air the reed moves, not its pitch. Low reeds are long, high reeds are short.

On the spectrum diagram, the pitch ruler of post 1, the plucked reed’s stems (top, and in the demo above) are this spectrum: 1\times, then 6.27\times, off the gray lines. The blown reed’s stems (bottom) sit at 1\times, 2\times, 3\times, 4\times, \dots, every one on a line, and none at 6.27\times. Each stem’s height is how strong that frequency is in the sound. Same reed, same operator; only the way it is played differs.


  
  
  Plucked (top): 1× and 6.27×, off the lines (17.55× is off the right edge). Blown (bottom): every stem on a line, none at 6.27×.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
Plucked: a ringing reed
A plucked reed rings like a kalimba tine. It moves as \sum_n a_n e^{-t/\tau_n} X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), so its sound is a sum of partials at the spectrum’s frequencies f_n, each fading at its own rate. The overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the fundamental are off the lines and die fast, as on the kalimba; the demo’s plucked sound is made exactly this way, with illustrative fading times.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
Blown: a sustained reed
Playing frequency: just below the reed’s own. Blow, and the reed swings through its slot, opening and closing the air path hundreds of times a second. It becomes a valve, and the sound comes mainly from the chopped airflow: the acoustics writer Colin Pykett notes that very little comes from the reed’s own motion. A steadily blown reed settles into a motion that repeats itself exactly, at a playing frequency f_p slightly below its first mode’s frequency, so the puffs of air repeat at that rate too. That the playing frequency sits below the reed’s own is observed in studies of blown reeds, not derived here: the physicist James Cottingham, reviewing that work, reports that “the sounding frequency of the blown reed is somewhat below the natural vibrating frequency of the reed tongue”, for the kind of reed that sounds in ordinary blowing and drawing on a harmonica. So the reed’s first mode sets the pitch, and changing the reed retunes the note.
Waveform: whole-number multiples. Why the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, and reproduced by computer models of reeds, but not derived here (fold below). Granting that it does, the rest is mathematics:

The airflow repeats. Let q(t) be the airflow through the slot. In the steady oscillation it repeats every P = 1/f_p seconds: q(t + P) = q(t).
A repeating signal has only whole-number multiples. Any reasonable function of period P is a sum of \cos(2\pi nt/P) and \sin(2\pi nt/P) for n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, its Fourier series, so it contains only the frequencies n f_p (post 1 proves the matching statement for a finite sum of partials).
So the note lands on the lines. The blown sound has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, with both odd and even multiples strongly represented (Pykett). How strong each one is depends on the shape of a single puff: short, sharp puffs give strong high partials.

The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up. That is why the reed’s own overtone frequencies, 6.27 and 17.55 times f_1, do not appear in a steadily blown note: that is where they went.



DetailsWhy the reed locks into one repeating motion, and how the demo makes its sound

A steady oscillation kept going by a steady push, like this one, is called a self-sustained oscillation, and the repeating cycle it settles into a limit cycle; the bowed string and the clarinet reed are others, and post 3 gives the smallest example. That the blown reed settles into one is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds; it is not derived here. A plausible picture, not a derivation: the airflow feeds energy mainly into the first mode, the other modes are not kept going at their own frequencies, and in the repeating cycle they move only as they are pushed, at whole-number multiples of f_p.
The demos’ blown sounds are models. The “Blow the C5 reed” and filing demos play one puff shape, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short, repeated at the playing frequency: its whole-number multiples weaker overall as they go up. The chromatic harmonica further down passes the same puff train through two broad peaks, a stand-in for resonances of the player’s mouth and the instrument, and adds a little band-passed breath noise. The peaks were set by ear, not measured, so the timbre is approximate. The pitch and the whole-number spacing are not approximations.


Tuning a reed with a file. Since the reed’s first mode sets the pitch, reed makers tune by scraping metal off, and where they scrape decides the direction. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thin the reed near the rivet and you remove stiffness where it counts: the pitch drops. Thin it near the tip and you remove mass where it counts: the pitch rises. It is the mass on a spring of post 2 again, whose frequency grows with stiffness and falls with mass. Try it below.


    Where to filebase
    
    Blow the filed reedBlow the original
    Filing removes a quarter of the thickness over about a tenth of the reed. The pitch change is estimated as in the fold below.
  




Step-by-step derivationWhy filing moves the pitch: stiffness against mass uses integration by parts and a first-order approximation

The Rayleigh quotient explains the direction. For the first mode, 
\omega_1^2 = \min_{u} \frac{\int_0^L EI\,(u'')^2\,dx}{\int_0^L \rho S\,u^2\,dx},
 the minimum taken over shapes, not identically zero, that satisfy the conditions at the rivet; the minimizing shape is the first mode itself. This is \omega^2 = k/m for a mass on a spring again: stiffness on top, weighted by where the reed bends, and mass at the bottom, weighted by where it moves. The steps below make this quantitative.

The quotient. Multiply \rho S\,\omega^2X = (EI\,X'')'' by X and integrate by parts twice; the boundary terms vanish at the rivet and at the free tip. This gives \omega^2 = \int EI(X'')^2 / \int \rho S X^2 for every mode.
Small change. File the reed so that its thickness changes by \delta h(x) < 0. Then I \propto h^3 changes by \delta(EI) = 3EI\,\delta h/h, and S \propto h changes by \delta(\rho S) = \rho S\,\delta h/h, to first order, that is, ignoring terms in (\delta h)^2.
First order. Because the first mode minimizes the quotient, changing the shape slightly changes the quotient only by an amount proportional to the square of the change. So to first order one may keep the old mode shape X and change only the coefficients: 
\delta(\omega^2) = \frac{\int \frac{\delta h}{h}\,\big(3EI\,(X'')^2 - \omega^2\rho S\,X^2\big)\,dx}{\int \rho S\,X^2\,dx}.

Sign. Near the rivet X \approx 0 and X'' is largest, so the bracket is positive and, with \delta h < 0, \omega drops. Near the tip X'' = 0 and X is largest, so the bracket is negative and \omega rises. In between there is a point where filing changes nothing, to first order.

The demo uses the full quotient with the original mode shape, which is accurate to first order in the depth of filing.





DetailsThe player’s control: breath, speech and bending

The player’s control. The player’s breath sets how hard the air flows: the reed’s frequency hardly varies with the wind pressure, which changes its loudness, and the shape of each puff changes with the pressure too, and so does the tone (Pykett). A free reed is slow to start, because it loses little energy per cycle (Pykett), and the note lasts as long as the breath. Skilled players can bend some notes on a diatonic harmonica downward, by coupling the reeds to the resonances of their own mouth and throat (Cottingham): a case where the player does move the pitch.


The chromatic slide. A chromatic harmonica has two sets of reed chambers, the second tuned a semitone higher. Each hole has a blow reed, sounded by breathing out, and a draw reed, sounded by breathing in, in each set. Pushing the slide moves a perforated bar that closes one set and opens the other, so every note rises a semitone. In solo tuning, the usual layout for a chromatic harmonica, each group of four holes holds C, E, G, C on the blow and D, F, A, B on the draw. Here is a whole one to play.


  blow, breathing out (top row: keys 1 … =)draw, breathing in (bottom row: keys Q … ])
  
  
    Slide (hold, or Space)
    Press and hold a hole. Slide across holes to move between notes.
  
  Twelve holes in solo tuning (explained just above), from C4, middle C, up three octaves. Pushing the slide raises every note a semitone, by switching the air to a second set of reeds.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
What we hear
Blown, the reed’s own overtones are absent from the steady sound. Blowing turns the reed into a valve that chops the air into puffs, and the puffs repeat exactly; a sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of its rate, so 6.27× and 17.55× have nowhere to appear. Plucked, the same reed rings with its own spectrum, and you hear the off-line overtones until they die. Same operator, same spectrum: the periodic motion of a steady drive decides where a blown note’s partials sit.
The same mechanism drives the bowed string and the clarinet, whose own frequencies already sit on or near the lines, so there the resonator’s modes shape which partials are strong. A free reed’s own overtones are far off the lines, which lets you hear that the drive, not the reed’s own frequencies, decides where a blown note’s partials sit.

The four aspects


The harmonica reed’s four aspects, for the two ways of playing it.


Aspect
Plucked
Blown




Pitch
the fundamental f_1
the playing frequency, just below f_1; bent down on some notes by the player’s mouth


Loudness
how hard the reed is plucked
the wind pressure


Timbre
off-line overtones at the start, then the fundamental
strong odd and even partials, set by the shape of each puff, which changes with the pressure


Duration
the fundamental’s fading
as long as the breath, after a slow start

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
What we found
A harmonica reed has the kalimba tine’s operator and spectrum, 1 : 6.27 : 17.55; plucked, that is what you hear. Blown, it swings just below its lowest frequency and chops the air into identical puffs, and a sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples, so the steady note has nothing at 6.27× or 17.55×. Periodicity wins: the drive decides where a blown note’s partials sit, and the reed’s lowest mode its pitch.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:

References. C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023 (sound from the puffs, not the reed’s motion; odd and even harmonics; frequency nearly independent of wind pressure, which changes loudness and pulse shape; slow speech). J. Cottingham, Acoustics of free-reed instruments, Physics Today 64(3), 2011, 44–48, for the playing frequency below the reed’s natural frequency (p. 45) and pitch bending through the player’s vocal tract. Wikipedia, Free reed aerophone and Rayleigh quotient.

title: A Bicycle Wheel
What you hear
text: The Shape of a Sound · 2 · Where the equations come from → · Glossary

title: What you hear
text:
1 · A string and a drum
Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. Both are a stretched piece of material, set shaking. So why do they sound so different?


  
    
      ▶ Pluck a string
      
    
    
      ▶ Strike a drum
      
    
  
  Call this the pitch ruler. Its gray lines mark whole-number multiples, 1×, 2×, 3×, …, of one base frequency, here the lowest in each sound. Each blue stem is one frequency in the sound; taller means it starts stronger, for an idealized pluck and strike. Both objects are idealized: a perfectly flexible string at 196 Hz, plucked a fifth of the way along (so 5× is missing), and an ideal round drumhead whose lowest frequency is 140 Hz, struck about a third of the way out from its center. Their frequencies are computed for these ideal objects (post 4 works them out); the fading times are modelling choices.


The stems tell the two apart: the string’s sit on the lines, at exactly 1, 2, 3, … times the lowest; the drum’s sit at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, … times the lowest, and no frequency in the range we hear as pitch fits them all closely (§3). This post explains, without differential equations, why that decides between a note and a thud.

title: What you hear
text:
2 · Four aspects of a sound
Sound. The air pressure p(t) at a listener, as a function of time.
The simplest sound is a pure tone, the sound of a tuning fork: a pressure swing a\cos(2\pi f t + \varphi) about the average air pressure, with frequency f in hertz (cycles per second), size a, and phase \varphi, which says where in its cycle it starts.
Partial. One sinusoidal component of a sound, with its own frequency, size and fading.
The instrument’s own part of the sound, when it is left to ring after a pluck or a strike, is to a good approximation a sum of partials, each fading at its own rate: 
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\, e^{-t/\tau_k} \cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k),
 with frequencies f_k, starting sizes a_k, phases \varphi_k and fading times \tau_k (every \tau_k seconds, a partial shrinks by a factor of e \approx 2.7). Each partial comes from one of the instrument’s modes, a shape the object swings in at one frequency, such as a string swinging as one arc, or as two halves in opposite directions; the body and the room pass them on, adding some ringing of their own. Post 3 explains this form; what it leaves out, such as breath, is noise.
Harmonic. A partial at a whole-number multiple n \cdot f of a base frequency f: the n-th harmonic. (For a harmonic sound, the first overtone is the second harmonic.)
An overtone is any partial above the lowest; a harmonic sound is one whose partials are all harmonics of one base.
We hear four aspects, all perceptions measured by asking listeners: what follows is about hearing, not mathematics (Moore 2012; Plomp 1976).

Pitch
Pitch. A perception: how high or low a sound is, measured as the frequency of the pure tone that listeners match it to.
This is the standard definition (Moore 2012, chapter 6; ASA terminology, 11.01). Pitch that can carry a melody is heard for repetition rates (§3) from about 30 Hz (Pressnitzer, Patterson and Krumbholz 2001), and for pure tones up to 4 or 5 kHz (the traditional limit; Oxenham and colleagues 2011): the range we hear as pitch.


  ▶ Pure tone, 220 Hz▶ Partials at 220, 440, 660, … Hz▶ Pure tone, 440 Hz
  The second sound has ten partials, at 1, 2, …, 10 times 220 Hz, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/10. It sounds richer than the first and just as high, so its pitch is 220 Hz. The third is an octave higher.




Loudness
Loudness. A perception: how strong a sound seems. Mainly set by the sound pressure level; it also depends on frequency (equal-loudness contours, ISO 226) and on the spread of partials, and it grows roughly as a power of intensity (about twice as loud per 10 dB; Stevens).
In short, 10 dB more is ten times the power and sounds about twice as loud (Stevens 1957), and at the same level a low tone sounds quieter than a mid-range one (ISO 226); the fold gives the numbers.



DetailsLoudness: decibels, equal-loudness contours and the power law

The sound pressure level is 20\log_{10}(p_{\mathrm{rms}}/20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa}) decibels (dB), with p_{\mathrm{rms}} the root-mean-square pressure, the square root of the average squared pressure swing; the intensity, the power carried through each square metre, grows as p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2, so 10 dB more is ten times the intensity. By the equal-loudness contours of ISO 226, which give the level at which pure tones of each frequency sound equally loud to young listeners, a 100 Hz tone needs about 79 dB to match a 1 kHz tone at 60 dB. At equal intensity, partials spread beyond a certain width in frequency sound louder than partials bunched together (Zwicker, Flottorp and Stevens 1957); and loudness grows roughly as the 0.3 power of intensity, so 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud, since 10^{0.3} \approx 2 (Stevens 1957).




  Same size of pressure swing:▶ 100 Hz▶ 1000 Hz▶ 3000 Hz▶ All three in turn
  1000 Hz, three levels:▶ 0, then −10, then −20 dB
  First row: three pure tones with exactly the same size of pressure swing in the signal. With good headphones the 100 Hz tone sounds much quieter than the other two; that is the ear's equal-loudness contour. Small laptop and phone speakers play 100 Hz weakly, which exaggerates the effect, and the level at your ear depends on your volume setting, so the numbers in the text apply only roughly. Second row: one tone, stepped down by 10 dB twice; each step sounds about half as loud.




Timbre
Timbre. What distinguishes sounds that agree in pitch (if they have one), loudness and duration: which partials are present, their relative sizes, how far they sit from whole-number multiples, how the sound starts and fades (attack and decay), noise and transients that are not modes (bow noise, breath, hammer thump), and fixed resonances that stay put whatever note is played (formants: a violin’s body, a clarinet’s tone-hole cutoff).
Mostly timbre is the partials’ sizes and how they change, the start especially (Wikipedia, Timbre; Moore 2012, chapter 8); the fold gives the evidence and the formants.



DetailsTimbre: the evidence, and the formants

The standard definition is shorter: what tells apart two sounds of the same loudness and pitch (ASA terminology, 12.09). Mostly it is the partials’ sizes and how they change (Wikipedia, Timbre; Moore 2012, chapter 8); removing the onsets of recorded instrument tones cut listeners’ accuracy at naming the instruments by about 15 percentage points (Saldanha and Corso 1964, summarized by Siedenburg 2019). Listeners also hear a finger hitting a piano key and the key hitting bottom (Goebl, Bresin and Fujinaga 2014). A violin’s body favors certain bands of frequency whatever the note, as a voice’s formants do (Schleske); above a cutoff frequency, roughly 1 to 1.5 kHz on a clarinet, sound waves travel on past the open tone holes instead of being turned back by them, and that cutoff depends little on the fingering (Moers and Kergomard 2011; Wolfe, clarinet acoustics).




  ▶ Pure tone▶ Every harmonic▶ Odd harmonics only▶ Every harmonic, plucked
  Four sounds with the same pitch, 220 Hz. The first three are steady and have the same power, which makes them roughly, not exactly, equally loud: one partial; twelve harmonics with sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3, …; and the odd ones of those, which sounds hollow, like a clarinet. The fourth has the second's partials but starts suddenly and fades, the higher partials faster, like a pluck.




Duration
Duration. How long a note sounds. For a ringing instrument: its fading times and when the player damps it (key release, mute, a hand or leg on the head). For a bowed or blown instrument: as long as the player keeps going.
How a note fades is part of its timbre; how long it lasts is its duration. A bass drummer stops a note with a leg or a towel on the head (Aleo, Interlochen 2023).


  Plucked:▶ Let it ring▶ Damp it after 0.35 s
  Bowed:▶ Half a second▶ Two seconds
  A string at 196 Hz. Plucked, it fades on its own unless damped; the damped note has the same partials, all made to die within about a tenth of a second. Bowed, it is a steady tone (partials 1, 1/2, 1/3, … of a repeating motion, §5) that lasts as long as the bow moves.



From the partials to the four aspects. For an instrument left to ring, the four aspects are heard from three lists, the frequencies f_k, the sizes a_k and the fading times \tau_k, through the ear’s own weighting: pitch mainly from where the f_k sit; loudness from the sizes, weighted by frequency; timbre from all three lists, especially early on, plus noise that is not a mode; duration from the fading and from when the player stops or damps the note. Bowed and blown instruments are different (§5).

The rest of this post asks where the f_k must sit for a clear pitch.

title: What you hear
text:
3 · Why whole numbers repeat
A sum of steady partials repeats exactly when all its frequencies are whole-number multiples of one frequency, and then at the largest such frequency. A signal p is periodic with period P > 0 if p(t+P) = p(t) for every t.

Proposition (repetition and whole numbers). Let p(t) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k), with distinct frequencies f_k > 0 and sizes a_k \ne 0. A time P > 0 is a period of p exactly when every f_k is a whole-number multiple of 1/P. So p is periodic exactly when every ratio f_k/f_1 is a fraction, and then its shortest period is 1/g, where g is the largest frequency of which every f_k is a whole-number multiple.
In words: steady partials add up to a sound that repeats only if they all sit on the lines of one pitch ruler, and it repeats at the base of the coarsest such ruler.

The smallest case is two pure tones with frequency ratio f_2/f_1 = j/k, a fraction in lowest terms. After P = k/f_1 seconds the lower tone has completed f_1P = k whole cycles and the upper one f_2P = j, so the sum begins again: it repeats every k cycles of the lower tone, at the rate g = f_1/k. At 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, that is every 100 cycles: 2.2 times a second for a lower tone at 220 Hz, far below the pitch range. That the sum repeats only for fractions needs one more fact, that sinusoids of different frequencies cannot cancel one another (the fold).


  ▶ 2 : 1▶ 3 : 2▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)Play the slider's ratio
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Two pure tones, the lower at 220 Hz. Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1 it lines up only after 100 cycles, far off the right of this picture.





ProofThe proposition: sinusoids of different frequencies are independent, so a period must fit every partial uses integrals of products of cosines, and divisibility

Lemma. Let 0 < g_1 < \dots < g_m, and suppose that c + \sum_{j=1}^m \big(\alpha_j\cos(2\pi g_j t) + \beta_j\sin(2\pi g_j t)\big) = 0 for every t. Then c = 0 and every \alpha_j and \beta_j is 0.
Proof of the lemma. For a function h, write \langle h\rangle = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T} h(t)\,dt for its long-run average, when the limit exists. For \gamma \ne 0, \int_{-T}^{T}\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\,dt = \sin(2\pi\gamma T)/(\pi\gamma) stays bounded as T grows, so \langle\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\rangle = 0; and \langle 1\rangle = 1. The product formulas 2\cos x\cos y = \cos(x-y) + \cos(x+y) and 2\sin x\sin y = \cos(x-y) - \cos(x+y) then give, for a, b > 0, \langle\cos(2\pi a t)\cos(2\pi b t)\rangle = \langle\sin(2\pi a t)\sin(2\pi b t)\rangle = \tfrac12 if a = b and 0 if a \ne b. A product of a sine and a cosine is an odd function, so its integral over [-T, T] is 0, and so is its average. Multiply the assumed identity by \cos(2\pi g_j t) and average: every term vanishes except \alpha_j/2, by the averages just computed, so \alpha_j = 0. Multiplying by \sin(2\pi g_j t) gives \beta_j = 0 in the same way. What remains is c = 0.
Proof of the proposition. If every f_kP is a whole number, each cosine completes whole cycles in time P, so p(t + P) = p(t). Conversely, suppose p(t+P) = p(t) for every t, and write \theta_k = 2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k and \delta_k = 2\pi f_k P. By the identity \cos(\theta + \delta) - \cos\theta = -2\sin(\delta/2)\sin(\theta + \delta/2), 
0 = p(t+P) - p(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n -2a_k\sin(\pi f_kP)\,\sin\!\big(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k + \pi f_kP\big).
 Expanding each term into \alpha_k\cos(2\pi f_k t) + \beta_k\sin(2\pi f_k t) gives \alpha_k^2 + \beta_k^2 = 4a_k^2\sin^2(\pi f_kP). The lemma, with c = 0, makes every \alpha_k and \beta_k zero, so a_k\sin(\pi f_kP) = 0; since a_k \ne 0 by hypothesis, \sin(\pi f_k P) = 0, which means f_kP is a whole number. This proves the first sentence.
The shortest period. If p has a period P, the first sentence makes every f_kP a whole number, so f_k/f_1 = (f_kP)/(f_1P) is a fraction. Conversely, suppose every f_k/f_1 is a fraction. Over a common denominator N, f_k = n_k h with h = f_1/N and whole numbers n_k. Let d be the greatest common divisor of n_1, \dots, n_n and g = dh; then f_k = m_kg with whole numbers m_k = n_k/d whose greatest common divisor is 1. By the first sentence, P is a period exactly when every m_k\,gP is a whole number. If gP is a whole number, so is every m_k\,gP. Conversely, Bézout’s identity (whole numbers whose greatest common divisor is 1 have a combination with whole-number coefficients equal to 1) gives whole numbers u_k with \sum_k u_km_k = 1, so gP = \sum_k u_k\,(m_k\,gP) is a whole number. So the periods are exactly the whole-number multiples of 1/g, and the shortest is 1/g. Finally, if every f_k is a whole-number multiple of some g', then 1/g' is a period, hence a multiple of 1/g, so g' \le g: g is the largest such frequency.
Check on the examples. Partials at 440, 660 and 880 Hz have h = 220, n_k = 2, 3, 4, d = 1, so g = 220 Hz although no partial sits there. Tones at 100 and 159 Hz have g = 1 Hz: the sum repeats once a second.


The repeating rate gets a name.
Repetition rate. For a sound whose partials are steady and exact whole-number multiples of a common frequency: 1 over its shortest period, which is the largest such common frequency. For partials that fade, or sit only near multiples: the largest frequency in the range we hear as pitch that they fit within a stated tolerance.
The second half covers real instruments. A sound that fades cannot repeat exactly, but it can nearly: if every partial sits on a multiple of g and fades with the same time \tau, each period is the one before shrunk by the factor e^{-1/(g\tau)}, by 0.45% at g = 220 Hz and \tau = 1 s. How near the multiples is near enough is a fact about hearing: a low partial mistuned by more than about 1 to 3%, depending on the listener, stands out as a separate tone (Moore, Glasberg and Peters 1986). Within 2%, the middle of that range, the lowest strong partials of §1’s drum fit no frequency above about 20 Hz, below the pitch range; the string’s fit 196 Hz exactly.



PreciselyHow the drum fails to fit, at different tolerances

Take the partials of the drum in §1 up to 3.2 times the lowest that start with at least a tenth of the strongest one’s size: 1, 1.593, 2.295, 2.653 and 3.155 times 140 Hz. (Its partials at 2.136 and 2.917 start with only about 2% of the strongest’s size, because the strike point or the listening point sits near a still line of their modes.) Call a frequency g a fit within a tolerance \epsilon if each partial lies within the fraction \epsilon of a whole-number multiple ng with n \ge 1. A computer search over g gives the largest fit; adding the drum’s higher partials could only lower it.



Tolerance
Largest fit g




1%
about 14 Hz


2%
about 20 Hz


3%
about 46 Hz



Why a fading sound cannot repeat exactly. If p(t+P) = p(t) for every t, then p(t) = p(t + mP) for every whole number m, and for a sound that dies away this tends to 0 as m grows, so p is zero. A piano’s partials, slightly sharp of the lines, also nearly repeat.
Within 3%, a base of about 46 Hz fits as its 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th and 10th multiples, each off by up to 3%, with nothing at the base or at its 2nd or 4th multiple. The 3% figure is generous. It comes from a different measurement by the same authors: in an earlier study, a single mistuned low partial of an otherwise exact harmonic sound kept counting fully toward its pitch up to about 3% (Moore, Glasberg and Peters 1985, as summarized by Darwin, Buffa and Smits 1990), whereas the 1 to 3% of §3 is where a partial starts to be heard out on its own (their 1986 study), and here every partial is off at once. What the ear makes of such a sound is a question about hearing; in the demo of §1, it is a thud.

title: What you hear
text:
4 · The missing fundamental
For a single tone, the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch, even when no partial sits at it. Play the note, then the same note without its 220 Hz partial, and watch the wave.


  
    ▶ The note▶ Without its 220 Hz partial
    Play again
  
  
  
  
  Mix your own
    Pure toneHollow, like a clarinet
    
  
  The wave over three cycles of 220 Hz; gray ticks mark each 1/220 of a second. Stems: how strong each partial is, at 1, 2, 3, … times 220 Hz, on the pitch ruler. The readout gives the repetition rate, the largest frequency of which every partial present is a whole-number multiple.


The wave changes shape but still repeats every 1/220 of a second, since 440, 660, 880, … Hz are all multiples of 220 Hz, and the pitch stays. Hearing the pitch without its fundamental is the missing-fundamental effect; it keeps a deep voice’s pitch over a telephone that carries little below about 300 Hz (Wikipedia, Missing fundamental). Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8× in “Mix your own”, and the pitch jumps an octave.
This finding about hearing (Moore 2012, chapter 6) relates the two notions:
Pitch and repetition rate. For a single tone whose prominent partials lie near a harmonic series in the pitch range, pitch ≈ that series’ base, even when its own partial is missing.

Beats
Two close partials fit no series in the pitch range; the ear hears one tone that swells and fades. For two pure tones of equal size, the sum-to-product formula gives 
\cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) = 2\cos\big(\pi (f_2 - f_1) t\big)\,\cos\big(\pi (f_1 + f_2) t\big),
 a tone at the average frequency whose size swells and fades |f_2 - f_1| times a second: beats. Tones at 220 and 222 Hz repeat together exactly twice a second, far below the pitch range; you hear a 221 Hz tone wobbling twice a second. Faster beats sound rough, and tones far enough apart sound as two smooth tones (Plomp and Levelt 1965).


  ▶ 220 + 222 Hz▶ 220 + 228 Hz▶ 220 + 245 Hz▶ 220 + 330 Hz
  
  
  The sum of two equal pure tones over one second. Its outline swells and shrinks as many times a second as the two frequencies differ: 2, 8 and 25 times; at 110 Hz apart the swells come too fast to see here, and you hear two smooth tones.




Exceptions to the pitch rule
The rule is about a single tone. Three kinds of sound break it.
Chords. The ear sorts the partials into several series and hears several pitches. C4 and G4 tuned to an exact 3 : 2 have all their partials on multiples of 130.8 Hz (C3), so together they repeat 130.8 times a second; yet you hear two notes, since the ear hears two sets of harmonics with different bases as two sounds (Bregman 1990).


  ▶ C4▶ G4▶ C4 and G4 together▶ C3, the pair's repetition rate
  Each note has eight harmonics, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/8: C4 at 261.6 Hz, G4 at exactly 3/2 of that, 392.4 Hz. Together they repeat 130.8 times a second, the rate of the last sound, which is not what the pair sounds like.


Bells and kettledrums. A harmonic subset sets the pitch, and the ear may choose an octave above the base. A bell is heard roughly an octave below its main partial, the nominal, often with no partial at the pitch heard (Hibbert); a kettledrum is named an octave above the base its main partials fit (HyperPhysics; kettledrum page). The fold gives the partials.
Strongly stretched partials. Partials running sharp of the lines, as on a stiff piano string, pull the pitch up (Jaatinen and Pätynen 2022); beyond the tolerance of §3, a partial is heard out on its own (Moore, Glasberg and Peters 1986).



DetailsThe bell’s and the kettledrum’s partials

In short. A bell’s strike note, the pitch it is heard at, is set mainly by three partials at nearly 2, 3 and 4 times its frequency, often with no partial exactly at it; its other main partials include the hum, an octave below, and the tierce, a minor third above, off the series. Without the tierce, the main partials fit the hum as base, yet the bell is heard an octave higher (Hibbert; Wikipedia, Strike tone). A kettledrum’s air pulls one set of its modes near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base, yet players name the note an octave higher, at the lowest of the set, the drum’s principal tone (HyperPhysics; Vienna’s Institute of Musical Acoustics).
The bell. In a well-tuned church bell the main partials, the hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal, sit near 0.5, 1, 1.2, 1.5 and 2 times the prime, and two more, the superquint and the octave nominal, near 3 and 4 times (Hibbert, upper partials); the strike note is close to the prime (Wikipedia, Strike tone). The nominal, superquint and octave nominal, nearly in the ratios 2 : 3 : 4, are heard as harmonics of a missing fundamental, the strike note, which lies roughly an octave below the nominal (Hibbert, strike note). It can differ from half the nominal by about a quarter of a semitone, and often no partial sits exactly at it, a puzzle Rayleigh noted in 1890; which partials set the note also depends on the bell’s size (Hibbert). Measured from the hum, the main partials sit at 1, 2, 2.4, 3, 4, 6 and 8: whole numbers, except the tierce.
The kettledrum. A kettledrum measured by Benade, tuned to C3, had its principal tone at 130.8 Hz and partials at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times it, close to 3, 4, 5 and 6 times half of it, together with others off this pattern (HyperPhysics, tabulating Benade). On C2, 65.4 Hz, that set forms a near-harmonic series, and HyperPhysics notes that the missing-fundamental effect might then give the pitch C2; the drum is named for its principal tone, C3. Vienna’s Institute of Musical Acoustics names the principal tone (“Grundton”) as the mode with one still line through the center, and notes that the drum’s many partials off whole-number ratios make its exact pitch hard to pin down.

title: What you hear
section: 5 · Four routes to a clear pitch
text:
5 · Four routes to a clear pitch
Instruments reach a clear pitch by four routes. A mode, in plain words, is a shape the object swings in at one frequency; each gives one partial.
1×2×3×

Modes on the whole numbers by nature: strings and air columns. The n-th mode fits n half-waves (the picture), and all waves travel at one speed, so an ideal string swings at exactly n times its lowest frequency; so does air in a flute (a clarinet: odd multiples). See the violin, clarinet and piano pages.
Modes moved there by design. The kettledrum’s air loading (drum page), the marimba bar’s undercut, the tabla’s loaded patch, and a bell’s profile, which puts all its principal partials but the minor-third tierce on whole-number multiples of one base.
Off-line partials suppressed. Weak or quick to die, as on a kalimba (kalimba page) or a glockenspiel, or never started, as where a timpanist strikes (a strike near a mode’s still line doesn’t start that mode).
A periodic drive: bow and breath. A motion that repeats has its partials at exact whole-number multiples, whatever the object’s own modes; the resonator’s modes shape which partials are strong (harmonica page).




DetailsThe four routes, with their sources


Modes on the whole numbers by nature: strings and air columns. A string’s n-th mode fits n half-waves between its ends (the picture), and every wave travels along the string at the same speed, so on an ideal string the n-th mode swings at exactly n times the lowest frequency. A flute’s air column, open at both ends, resonates at every whole-number multiple, and a clarinet’s, closed at the reed, at the odd ones (Wolfe). Guitars and harps take this route, and the piano nearly, since stiffness pushes its partials slightly sharp; bowed strings and winds start here, and route 4 makes their partials exact. See the violin, clarinet and piano pages.
Modes moved there by design. A kettledrum’s air slows its coarse shapes most, pulling one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 (drum page). A marimba bar’s arch, cut underneath, moves its first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, for a uniform bar, to 4 times; a xylophone’s shallower cut, to 3 times (HyperPhysics; Scavone). A patch of paste loading the middle of a tabla’s head brings its modes near whole-number ratios (Raman and Kumar 1920). Founders shape and tune a bell so that most of its principal partials sit on multiples of half the strike note, the minor-third tierce apart (series index).
Off-line partials suppressed. Some are weak or die fast: a kalimba tine’s overtones, at 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest, die within a fraction of a second (Chapman 2008; kalimba page), and a struck glockenspiel bar’s modes all die out quickly except the lowest (Scavone). Others are not started: a strike at a still point of a mode does not set that mode going, and timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, near the still lines of several modes that do not fit the note (the playing spot: HyperPhysics; the still lines: drum page).
A periodic drive: bow and breath. A bow or a breath keeps feeding the motion, which settles into a single repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples, whatever the object’s own modes (Wolfe, How harmonic are harmonics?; §3 proves this for a finite sum): a bow’s stick and slip drive all of a string’s resonances at exactly harmonic ratios, and a harmonica reed, whose own overtones are off the lines, chops the air into identical puffs (harmonica page). The resonator’s modes shape which partials are strong, and the player sets loudness and duration.





  1 · By nature:▶ Plucked string
  2 · By design:▶ Uniform bar▶ Undercut bar
  3 · Suppressed:▶ Kalimba tine▶ The same, overtones ringing as long
  4 · Driven:▶ Harmonica reed, plucked▶ The same reed, blown
  Row 2: a bar's lowest two partials at middle C, with the overtone at 2.76 times the lowest (a uniform bar) or at 4 times (an undercut marimba bar); sizes and fading times illustrative. Row 3: a kalimba tine at C5, its overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, fading fast as measured, then the same partials made to ring as long as the lowest. Row 4: the reed has the tine's frequencies when plucked; blown, it sounds a steady tone with partials at whole-number multiples only.


Why does a vibrating object have modes at all, and why do their frequencies form a list? That is the mathematical answer, post 3.

title: What you hear
text:
6 · Dynamics change timbre too
A harder blow sounds louder and brighter: a piano hammer’s felt gets harder the more it is squashed, so a fast hammer stays on the string for a shorter time and starts more high partials (Askenfelt and Jansson 1990; Russell 1997); with a felt that stayed equally soft, a loud note would be a soft note turned up. Post 2 models the felt, and post 4’s piano page takes it up.


  ▶ Soft blow▶ Hard blow▶ Soft blow, turned up
  Middle C on a model piano string. The hard blow has stronger high partials and an average level 10 dB higher; the third button plays the soft blow 10 dB louder, at the hard blow's average level, and it still sounds duller. How fast the partials fall off with number is an illustrative choice, not computed from a model of the felt.

title: What you hear
text:
What we found
A clear pitch is a matter of where the partials sit: at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the pitch range, so the sound nearly repeats at the largest such rate, which the ear hears as the pitch of a single tone, chords, bells, kettledrums and stretched partials aside. A string’s partials sit on the lines and a piano’s very nearly; an ideal drum’s fit nothing in the pitch range.

title: What you hear
text:
